questions.stem: Select all of the items that are part of the rights of medication administration.

options.text: Right provider
options.rationale: Near miss concept The prescriber matters to a valid order, but it is not one of the rights you check at the bedside.

options.text: Right dose
options.rationale: The ten rights are patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response, the right to refuse and education. Reason means the drug matches a condition the patient has. Response means you go back and evaluate the effect.

options.text: Right reason

questions.stem: When does the nurse perform the three checks of medication administration?

options.text: Before the first dose, after the first dose, and at discharge
options.rationale: Near miss concept These are monitoring points, not the three label checks.

options.text: At the start of the shift, at midday and at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept The checks are tied to handling the drug, not to the clock.

options.text: When taking it out, when preparing it, and at the bedside before giving
options.rationale: You compare the label with the medication record three times: when you pull it from the dispenser, when you prepare it, and at the bedside before you give it. Most errors are caught at the third check, with the patient in front of you.

options.text: When ordered, when dispensed by pharmacy, and when documented
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ordering and dispensing are other people's checks; yours happen while you handle the dose.

questions.takeaway: Pull, prepare, bedside.
questions.strategy: Each check happens with the drug in your hand.

questions.stem: Select all of the acceptable ways to identify a patient before giving a medication.

options.text: Ask the patient to state the full name
options.rationale: Use two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, stated by the patient and matched to the band. The medical record number on the band is also an accepted identifier. Never use the room number, and never ask a question the patient can answer with yes.

options.text: Ask the patient to state the date of birth
options.rationale: Use two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, stated by the patient and matched to the band. The medical record number on the band is also an accepted identifier. Never use the room number, and never ask a question the patient can answer with yes.

options.text: Check the room and bed number on the door sign against the record
options.rationale: Near miss concept Patients change rooms and beds; a location never identifies a person.

options.text: Compare the stated name and birth date with the band
options.rationale: Use two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, stated by the patient and matched to the band. The medical record number on the band is also an accepted identifier. Never use the room number, and never ask a question the patient can answer with yes.

options.text: Ask, "Are you Alex Lopez?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept A yes or no question invites a confused or hard of hearing patient to say yes to the wrong name.

questions.strategy: Reject any option a patient could pass without knowing who they are.

questions.stem: Match each drug to the assessment the nurse completes right before giving it.
questions.takeaway: Match the assessment to what the drug can do wrong. Insulin drops glucose. Beta blockers and diltiazem slow the heart and drop pressure. Furosemide wastes potassium. Opioids depress breathing, and sedation rises before breathing slows. Assess the thing the drug can push too far.
questions.strategy: Ask what this drug could do to harm the patient in the next hour, then pick the assessment that catches it.

questions.stem: A patient takes a drug that is metabolized by the liver. Which laboratory values should the nurse watch?

options.text: Creatinine and blood urea nitrogen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Creatinine and BUN track the kidneys, which excrete drugs.

options.text: ALT and AST
options.rationale: The liver metabolizes most drugs. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are liver enzymes that rise when liver cells are damaged. If they rise, the drug can build up or the drug itself may be injuring the liver.

options.text: Hemoglobin and hematocrit
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Blood counts do not reflect how the liver handles a drug.

options.text: Sodium and potassium
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Electrolytes do not show liver injury.

questions.takeaway: Liver: ALT and AST. Kidneys: creatinine.
questions.strategy: Pair the organ with its marker.

questions.stem: A patient's creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.1 mg/dL. Why does this matter for drugs cleared by the kidneys?

options.text: The drug will need to be given by a different route
options.rationale: Near miss concept Changing the route does not fix poor excretion; the dose or drug changes.

options.text: The drug will be absorbed more slowly from the gut
options.rationale: Near miss concept Absorption happens in the gut; creatinine reflects excretion.

options.text: The drug will be metabolized faster by the liver
options.rationale: Near miss concept The liver does not speed up to make up for the kidneys.

options.text: The drug can build up to toxic levels
options.rationale: Creatinine rises when the kidneys filter less. A drug the kidneys excrete then stays in the blood longer, and each dose stacks on the last. The dose often needs lowering, so you report the rise before the next dose.

questions.takeaway: Rising creatinine, stacking drug.
questions.strategy: Follow the drug from absorption to excretion and find the step the lab measures.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about drug levels.
questions.sentence: The peak is the [[1]] level of the drug in the blood. The trough is the [[2]] level, and it is drawn [[3]].

options.text: average
highest
lowest
lowest
highest
average
one hour after the dose
at the same time as the peak
right before the next dose

questions.takeaway: The peak is the highest level, reached after the drug is absorbed or infused. The trough is the lowest level, just before the next dose is due. A trough that is too high means the drug is not clearing and toxicity is building. Trough: right before the next dose.
questions.strategy: Trough sounds like low; it is the bottom of the curve, just before the next dose lifts it.

questions.stem: Match each finding to the nurse's correct action.
columns: Anaphylaxis: stop, airway, epinephrine per order

rows.text: Hives and itching 30 minutes after a first dose of amoxicillin
Mild nausea after an oral antibiotic taken on an empty stomach
Throat tightness, wheezing and a blood pressure of 82/50 after an IV antibiotic
rows.answer: Anaphylaxis: stop, airway, epinephrine per order

rows.text: An apical pulse of 46 before a scheduled beta blocker

answer.r3: Anaphylaxis: stop, airway, epinephrine per order

questions.takeaway: A side effect is expected and managed, such as giving the drug with food. An adverse or toxic effect is harmful, so you hold and tell the provider. An allergy is an immune reaction, so the drug stops and the allergy goes in the record. Anaphylaxis threatens the airway and circulation, so you stop the drug, support the airway and give epinephrine per order. Expected, harmful, immune, life threatening: four different actions.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions: is it expected, and is it immune? Then ask whether the airway or blood pressure is involved.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates a side effect from an allergy?

options.text: A side effect is an immune response; an allergy is expected
options.rationale: Near miss concept This reverses the two.

options.text: An allergy always causes anaphylaxis, while a side effect never causes harm
options.rationale: Absolute language Allergies range from rash to anaphylaxis, and some side effects are serious.

options.text: A side effect is predictable from the drug; an allergy is immune
options.rationale: A side effect comes from the drug's own action and can be predicted, like a cough from an ACE inhibitor. An allergy is the immune system reacting to the drug, like hives from penicillin. Recording a side effect as an allergy can block a useful drug later.

options.text: Both are the same and are documented as allergies
options.rationale: Near miss concept Charting nausea as an allergy can deny the patient a drug they need later.

questions.takeaway: Side effect = the drug's action. Allergy = the immune system.
questions.strategy: Look for the mechanism, not the severity.

questions.stem: Select all of the medications considered high alert.

options.text: Regular insulin
options.rationale: High alert drugs cause serious harm when given wrong: insulin, anticoagulants such as heparin, opioids such as hydromorphone, and IV potassium. They get an independent double check per policy.

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acetaminophen needs a daily maximum but is not on the high alert list in this content.

options.text: Heparin infusion
options.rationale: High alert drugs cause serious harm when given wrong: insulin, anticoagulants such as heparin, opioids such as hydromorphone, and IV potassium. They get an independent double check per policy.

options.text: Hydromorphone
options.rationale: High alert drugs cause serious harm when given wrong: insulin, anticoagulants such as heparin, opioids such as hydromorphone, and IV potassium. They get an independent double check per policy.

options.text: IV potassium chloride
options.rationale: High alert drugs cause serious harm when given wrong: insulin, anticoagulants such as heparin, opioids such as hydromorphone, and IV potassium. They get an independent double check per policy.

options.text: Docusate
options.rationale: Near miss concept A stool softener carries little risk of serious harm.

questions.takeaway: Insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, IV potassium.
questions.strategy: Ask which error would kill fastest.

questions.stem: Why is IV potassium chloride never given by IV push?

options.text: A rapid rise in potassium can stop the heart
options.rationale: Potassium controls the electrical charge of heart cells. A bolus raises the level faster than the body can move it into cells, causing fatal dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest. It is always diluted and given on a pump at a controlled rate.

options.text: It precipitates in the IV tubing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Potassium does not precipitate in tubing.

options.text: It causes immediate hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Potassium does not lower glucose.

options.text: It is irritating to veins and causes painful phlebitis
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data It does irritate veins, but that is not why push is forbidden.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium: diluted, on a pump, never push.
questions.strategy: Pick the option that kills, not the one that irritates.

questions.stem: Select all of the medications the nurse should not crush.

options.text: Metoprolol succinate ER
options.rationale: Extended release forms (ER, XR, XL, SR, CR) would release the whole day's dose at once. Enteric coating protects the stomach or the drug from acid. Sublingual tablets are meant to dissolve under the tongue. When in doubt, ask pharmacy.

options.text: Aspirin enteric coated
options.rationale: Extended release forms (ER, XR, XL, SR, CR) would release the whole day's dose at once. Enteric coating protects the stomach or the drug from acid. Sublingual tablets are meant to dissolve under the tongue. When in doubt, ask pharmacy.

options.text: Nifedipine XL
options.rationale: Extended release forms (ER, XR, XL, SR, CR) would release the whole day's dose at once. Enteric coating protects the stomach or the drug from acid. Sublingual tablets are meant to dissolve under the tongue. When in doubt, ask pharmacy.

options.text: Furosemide tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept A plain immediate release tablet can usually be crushed.

options.text: Nitroglycerin sublingual
options.rationale: Extended release forms (ER, XR, XL, SR, CR) would release the whole day's dose at once. Enteric coating protects the stomach or the drug from acid. Sublingual tablets are meant to dissolve under the tongue. When in doubt, ask pharmacy.

options.text: Lisinopril tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept A plain immediate release tablet can usually be crushed.

questions.takeaway: Letters after the name, a coating, or under the tongue: do not crush.
questions.strategy: Look for a suffix or a delivery method on the label.

questions.stem: What happens if an extended release tablet is crushed?

options.text: The drug stops working completely
options.rationale: Near miss concept The drug still works, too much and too fast.

options.text: The drug cannot be absorbed by the gut
options.rationale: Near miss concept Absorption is faster, not blocked.

options.text: The full dose is released at once
options.rationale: An extended release tablet is built to release its dose over 12 to 24 hours. Crushing it breaks that design, so the whole dose is absorbed at once, causing a high peak and toxicity, followed by a gap with no drug.

options.text: The drug becomes an allergen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Crushing does not create an allergy.

questions.takeaway: Crushed ER = dose dumping.
questions.strategy: Think about what the special form was built to do.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes a patient received the wrong dose. Place the actions in order.

options.text: File the incident report per policy
Notify the provider
Document the patient's condition and care given
Assess the patient

questions.takeaway: The patient comes first, so you assess for harm. Then the provider, who decides on treatment. Then you chart the facts of the patient's condition and care. The incident report is filed last and is never mentioned in the chart. Patient, provider, chart, report.
questions.strategy: Put the patient before the paperwork every time.

questions.stem: Where is the incident report for a medication error recorded?

options.text: Separately, and it is not mentioned in the chart
options.rationale: The incident report is an internal quality tool. It is filed separately and never mentioned in the medical record. The chart records only the facts: what was given, the patient's condition and what was done.

options.text: In the nursing care plan as a safety problem
options.rationale: Near miss concept The care plan addresses patient problems, not event reports.

options.text: In the progress notes, with a copy in the medication record
options.rationale: Near miss concept Referencing the report in the chart turns a quality tool into part of the legal record.

options.text: In the medication record, next to the dose given
options.rationale: Near miss concept The chart gets the facts of what was given and the patient's response, not the report.

questions.takeaway: Facts in the chart. Report outside the chart.
questions.strategy: Separate the legal record from the quality process.

questions.stem: A patient who has trouble swallowing has an order for metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg PO daily, crushed in applesauce. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it whole with extra water and watch the patient swallow closely
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Swallowing whole avoids dose dumping but ignores the swallowing problem the order was trying to solve.

options.text: Hold it and clarify the form with pharmacy or the provider
options.rationale: Crushing extended release metoprolol dumps the full daily dose, which can cause severe bradycardia and hypotension. The nurse holds and clarifies. Pharmacy can suggest another form, such as metoprolol tartrate given twice daily.

options.text: Crush it, since applesauce makes it easier to swallow
options.rationale: Institution as rationale The order says crush, but an order does not make crushing an ER tablet safe.

options.text: Cut the tablet in half and give both halves
options.rationale: Near miss concept Splitting can also damage the release design unless the tablet is scored for it.

questions.takeaway: An order to crush an ER drug is an order to clarify.
questions.strategy: When the order itself is unsafe, the answer is to clarify, not to follow.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after the first dose of IV ampicillin, a patient has hives, a hoarse voice and wheezing. SpO2 has fallen from 97% to 90%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Recheck the vital signs in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature A hoarse voice and wheezing are airway changes; waiting is not safe.

options.text: Stop the infusion and call for help
options.rationale: Hives with hoarseness, wheezing and a falling saturation is anaphylaxis. You stop the drug, call for help, support the airway and give epinephrine per order. Epinephrine is the first line drug because it opens the airway and raises the blood pressure.

options.text: Give the ordered oral diphenhydramine
options.rationale: Correct but premature An antihistamine treats the hives but will not open a closing airway.

options.text: Document the allergy in the record
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The allergy must be charted, after the patient is safe.

questions.takeaway: Airway signs after a drug = stop it and get help.
questions.strategy: Pick the action that stops the exposure and brings resources.

questions.stem: A patient receives IV vancomycin every 12 hours. The next dose is due at 2100, and a trough level is ordered. When should the trough be drawn?

options.text: At 1500, halfway between doses
options.rationale: Near miss concept A midpoint level is neither peak nor trough.

options.text: With the morning labs at 0500
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Lab convenience does not change when the trough must be drawn.

options.text: Right before the 2100 dose
options.rationale: The trough is the lowest level, so it is drawn right before the next dose, usually within 30 minutes. If it is high, the drug is not clearing, and the provider may change the dose before it is given.

options.text: One hour after the 2100 dose ends
options.rationale: Near miss concept That timing measures a peak.

questions.takeaway: Trough: just before the next dose. Hold the dose until it is drawn.
questions.strategy: Match the name to the shape of the curve.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a patient metoprolol 50 mg instead of the ordered 25 mg. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check the apical pulse and blood pressure
options.rationale: Too much beta blocker slows the heart and lowers blood pressure. You assess those first, then notify the provider, chart the patient's condition and file the report.

options.text: Document that the wrong dose was given
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documentation follows assessment and notification.

options.text: Complete an incident report while the details are fresh
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The report matters but comes after the patient.

options.text: Notify the charge nurse about the error
options.rationale: Correct but premature Reporting is needed, but the patient may already be bradycardic.

questions.takeaway: After an error, assess the patient for exactly what the drug does.
questions.strategy: Patient before process.

questions.stem: A nurse enters room 12 with medications. The patient has no identification band and says, "I am in bed A." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the drugs until a band is applied and two identifiers match
options.rationale: Without a band, two identifiers cannot be confirmed against the record. The nurse holds, gets a band applied, and then matches name and date of birth stated by the patient.

options.text: Ask the roommate to confirm the patient's name
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope A roommate is not a valid identifier and breaches privacy.

options.text: Give them, since the room and bed match
options.rationale: Near miss concept Room and bed are locations, not identifiers.

options.text: Ask the patient to confirm the name printed on the medication label
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reading a name to the patient invites a yes.

questions.takeaway: No band, no meds.
questions.strategy: Reject any check that does not match the patient to the record.

questions.stem: Why is hypertension treated even when the patient has no symptoms?

options.text: Untreated high pressure always causes a stroke within the first year
options.rationale: Absolute language Risk rises over years; always and within a year overstate it.

options.text: Treatment relieves the headaches it commonly causes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Most patients with hypertension have no headaches; symptoms are not the reason to treat.

options.text: High pressure damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over time
options.rationale: Persistently high arterial pressure strains the heart, damages vessel walls in the brain and kidneys and harms the retina. Because it is usually silent, the only way to know it is controlled is to measure it.

options.text: Treatment cures the underlying cause of the high pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Primary hypertension is managed for life, not cured.

questions.takeaway: Silent does not mean safe.
questions.strategy: Choose the option about long term organ damage, not symptoms.

questions.stem: Select all of the drug classes that are first line for most patients with uncomplicated hypertension.

options.text: Beta blocker
options.rationale: Near miss concept Beta blockers are added when there is a specific reason: after MI, heart failure or atrial fibrillation.

options.text: Thiazide diuretic
options.rationale: First line drugs for most patients are a thiazide, an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a calcium channel blocker. They lower pressure and reduce the risk of stroke and MI. Beta blockers and spironolactone are added for a specific reason.

options.text: Potassium sparing diuretic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spironolactone is added when pressure stays hard to control.

options.text: ACE inhibitor
options.rationale: First line drugs for most patients are a thiazide, an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a calcium channel blocker. They lower pressure and reduce the risk of stroke and MI. Beta blockers and spironolactone are added for a specific reason.

options.text: Calcium channel blocker
options.rationale: First line drugs for most patients are a thiazide, an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a calcium channel blocker. They lower pressure and reduce the risk of stroke and MI. Beta blockers and spironolactone are added for a specific reason.

options.text: Angiotensin II receptor blocker
options.rationale: First line drugs for most patients are a thiazide, an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a calcium channel blocker. They lower pressure and reduce the risk of stroke and MI. Beta blockers and spironolactone are added for a specific reason.

questions.takeaway: First line: thiazide, pril or sartan, dipine.
questions.strategy: Separate first line from added for a reason.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the drug added for it.

rows.text: Pressure still high on three drugs at full doses
New uncomplicated hypertension in a healthy adult

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers are added after MI, in heart failure and in atrial fibrillation because they slow the heart and lower oxygen demand. Spironolactone is added for resistant hypertension. Uncomplicated hypertension starts with a first line drug. Beta blockers need a cardiac reason.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the heart itself needs slowing.

questions.stem: Select all of the steps for an accurate blood pressure measurement.

options.text: Use a cuff whose bladder fits the arm
options.rationale: Use the right cuff size, seat the patient for 5 minutes with feet flat and back supported, and support the arm at heart level. A cuff too small or an arm hanging down both read falsely high and can lead to overtreatment.

options.text: Have the patient seated and resting for 5 minutes
options.rationale: Use the right cuff size, seat the patient for 5 minutes with feet flat and back supported, and support the arm at heart level. A cuff too small or an arm hanging down both read falsely high and can lead to overtreatment.

options.text: Support the arm at heart level
options.rationale: Use the right cuff size, seat the patient for 5 minutes with feet flat and back supported, and support the arm at heart level. A cuff too small or an arm hanging down both read falsely high and can lead to overtreatment.

options.text: Measure right after the patient walks in
options.rationale: Near miss concept Activity raises the reading; the patient should rest first.

options.text: Let the arm hang at the side
options.rationale: Near miss concept An arm below heart level reads falsely high.

options.text: Keep the feet flat and the back supported
options.rationale: Use the right cuff size, seat the patient for 5 minutes with feet flat and back supported, and support the arm at heart level. A cuff too small or an arm hanging down both read falsely high and can lead to overtreatment.

questions.takeaway: Right cuff, rest 5 minutes, arm at heart level.
questions.strategy: Every wrong step makes the number read high.

questions.stem: A nurse uses a cuff that is too small for the patient's arm. How will this affect the reading?

options.text: It will read falsely low
options.rationale: Near miss concept A cuff too large reads low; too small reads high.

options.text: It will read falsely high
options.rationale: A small cuff needs more pressure to squeeze the artery closed, so the reading is falsely high. That can lead to a drug the patient does not need or a dose that is too high.

options.text: It will be accurate if taken twice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Repeating with the wrong cuff repeats the error.

options.text: It will show a wide pulse pressure only
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Pulse pressure is not the main effect of cuff size.

questions.takeaway: Small cuff, high number.
questions.strategy: Think about how hard the cuff must squeeze.

questions.stem: Match each drug to where it mainly lowers blood pressure.
columns: The volume: fluid in the system

rows.answer: The volume: fluid in the system
The volume: fluid in the system

answer.r3: The volume: fluid in the system
answer.r6: The volume: fluid in the system

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers, diltiazem and verapamil slow the heart. Dipine calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and nitrates relax the vessels. Diuretics remove volume, and spironolactone blocks the hormone that holds it. Heart, vessels, volume.
questions.strategy: Name the target, then the drug class falls in place.

questions.stem: Place the steps of the renin angiotensin aldosterone system in order.

options.text: Angiotensin converting enzyme converts it to angiotensin II
Angiotensin I forms, which is inactive
Vessels tighten and aldosterone holds sodium and water
The kidneys release renin when blood flow drops

questions.takeaway: When the kidneys sense low pressure or flow, they release renin. Renin turns angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, which is inactive. ACE converts it to angiotensin II, which tightens vessels and triggers aldosterone. Aldosterone makes the kidneys hold sodium and water, raising volume and pressure. Renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, aldosterone.
questions.strategy: The chain starts at the kidney and ends at the kidney.

questions.stem: Match each drug to the step of the chain it blocks.
columns: Converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II

rows.answer: Converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II

answer.r3: Converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II

questions.takeaway: Prils block ACE, so less angiotensin II is made. Sartans let angiotensin II form but block its receptor. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone at the end of the chain. All three raise potassium, because aldosterone is what normally gets rid of it. pril blocks the enzyme, sartan the receptor, spironolactone the hormone.
questions.strategy: Locate each drug on the chain.

questions.stem: What does angiotensin II do to raise blood pressure?

options.text: It dilates vessels and increases urine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dilation and more urine would lower pressure.

options.text: It blocks sodium reabsorption in the kidney
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aldosterone, triggered by angiotensin II, increases sodium reabsorption.

options.text: It speeds the heart and releases renin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Renin comes before angiotensin II in the chain, not after it.

options.text: It tightens vessels and releases aldosterone
options.rationale: Angiotensin II is a strong vasoconstrictor and signals the adrenal gland to release aldosterone. Tighter vessels and more retained sodium and water both raise pressure. Blocking it is why prils and sartans work.

questions.takeaway: Angiotensin II: squeeze and hold.
questions.strategy: Pick the option where both effects raise pressure.

Beta blocker to lower oxygen demand
Beta blocker or diltiazem to control the rate
Switch from ACE inhibitor to ARB

rows.answer: ACE inhibitor or ARB to protect the kidneys

rows.text: A dry cough since starting lisinopril
rows.answer: Switch from ACE inhibitor to ARB

rows.answer: Beta blocker or diltiazem to control the rate

ACE inhibitor or ARB to protect the kidneys

answer.r1: ACE inhibitor or ARB to protect the kidneys
answer.r2: Switch from ACE inhibitor to ARB
answer.r3: Beta blocker or diltiazem to control the rate
answer.r4: Beta blocker to lower oxygen demand

questions.takeaway: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower pressure inside the kidney's filters and slow protein loss, so they protect the kidneys in diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Beta blockers slow the heart and lower oxygen demand after MI or with angina. Beta blockers or diltiazem slow conduction to control the rate in atrial fibrillation. ACE inhibitor cough comes from bradykinin, which ARBs do not build up. The condition picks the drug.
questions.strategy: Ask what the drug does that this patient specifically needs.

questions.topic: why this patient gets this drug
questions.stem: Why is an ACE inhibitor or ARB preferred for a patient with diabetes and hypertension?
questions.objective: why this patient gets this drug

options.text: It works faster than any other antihypertensive
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed is not the reason for the choice.

options.text: It lowers blood glucose along with blood pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept These drugs do not lower glucose.

options.text: It protects the kidneys and slows protein loss
options.rationale: Diabetes damages the kidney's filters. ACE inhibitors and ARBs relax the vessel leaving each filter, lowering the pressure inside it, which slows protein loss in the urine and the decline of kidney function.

options.text: It prevents low blood sugar episodes
options.rationale: Near miss concept They do not affect hypoglycemia; that is a beta blocker teaching point.

questions.takeaway: Diabetes or kidney disease: pril or sartan.
questions.strategy: Look for the organ the drug protects.

questions.stem: Which teaching applies to every antihypertensive?

options.text: Sit at the edge of the bed before standing and rise slowly
options.rationale: Every antihypertensive can cause orthostatic hypotension, a drop in pressure on standing. Dangling first and rising slowly let the body adjust, and fall precautions protect older adults.

options.text: Take it at bedtime to avoid daytime dizziness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Timing depends on the drug; diuretics, for example, go in the morning.

options.text: Skip it if you feel tired that morning
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Tiredness alone is not a reason to skip; report it instead.

options.text: Take it only on the days your home pressure reading is high
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure needs daily control; skipping causes swings.

questions.takeaway: All antihypertensives: dangle, rise slowly, prevent falls.
questions.strategy: Pick the safety measure that applies across the class.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about orthostatic vital signs.
questions.sentence: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in systolic pressure of at least [[1]] or in diastolic pressure of at least [[2]] within 3 minutes of standing. The nurse's first safety action is to [[3]].

options.text: 20 mm Hg
10 mm Hg
5 mm Hg
20 mm Hg
5 mm Hg
10 mm Hg
encourage walking to adapt
return the patient to sitting or lying
give the next dose early

questions.takeaway: A systolic drop of 20 or a diastolic drop of 10 within 3 minutes of standing is orthostatic hypotension. The patient sits or lies back down to restore blood flow to the brain, and you report the finding before the next antihypertensive. 20 down top, 10 down bottom, sit back down.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone; do not assume the two numbers match.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension says, "I stopped my amlodipine last month because I feel fine and never had symptoms anyway." Which response is best?

options.text: "You should restart it today at double the dose to catch up."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is the provider's decision and doubling is unsafe.

options.text: "It is your choice, but your provider will probably not be happy about it at all."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic This shames the patient without teaching anything.

options.text: "Then your pressure is probably controlled, so we will just recheck it."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Feeling fine says nothing about pressure.

options.text: "High pressure rarely causes symptoms, so only a reading tells us it is controlled."
options.rationale: Hypertension is usually silent, so feeling fine is not evidence of control. The nurse corrects the belief, checks the pressure and lets the provider know the drug was stopped.

questions.takeaway: Correct the belief, then measure.
questions.strategy: Find the option that addresses why the patient stopped.

questions.stem: A patient arrives late, rushes into the clinic and has a blood pressure of 168/96 in the left arm, which is hanging at the side. The last three readings were near 128/78. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Have the patient rest 5 minutes and recheck with the arm supported
options.rationale: Activity and an arm below heart level both raise the reading. With a stable history, the nurse repeats the measurement correctly before acting on it.

options.text: Give the next scheduled dose early
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Giving a dose early is not a nursing decision and the reading is unreliable.

options.text: Recheck immediately in the right arm while the patient is standing at the desk
options.rationale: Near miss concept Standing adds another error.

options.text: Report new uncontrolled hypertension to the provider
options.rationale: Correct but premature The reading was taken wrong; reporting it as new is premature.

questions.takeaway: Fix the technique before you treat the number.
questions.strategy: When the data is suspect, collect it again correctly.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has a blood pressure of 148/92 on two visits and protein in the urine. Kidney function is normal for now. Which drug should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Lisinopril, to protect the kidneys
options.rationale: Diabetes with protein in the urine points to early kidney damage. An ACE inhibitor (or an ARB) lowers pressure and slows the loss of protein and kidney function.

options.text: Spironolactone, for resistant pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept The pressure is not resistant; no drug has been tried.

options.text: Furosemide, for fluid overload
options.rationale: Near miss concept There is no fluid overload, and loops are not for long term pressure.

options.text: Metoprolol, to slow the heart
options.rationale: Near miss concept There is no MI, heart failure or atrial fibrillation to justify a beta blocker.

questions.takeaway: Diabetes plus protein in the urine: pril or sartan.
questions.strategy: Match the drug to the condition alongside the pressure.

questions.stem: An 82 year old started amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide this week. The patient reports dizziness when getting up at night to urinate. Lying blood pressure is 138/80 and standing is 112/70 after 2 minutes. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Encourage fast walking to the bathroom
Give both drugs at bedtime
Place a bedside commode and use fall precautions
Teach the patient to dangle before standing
Restrict fluids to 1 liter a day
Hypoglycemia
Orthostatic hypotension
Dehydration from poor intake
Transient ischemic attack
Standing blood pressure before doses
Serum glucose
Hemoglobin A1C
Pupil size
Falls and near falls

questions.takeaway: A systolic drop of 26 on standing is orthostatic hypotension, made worse by a new vasodilator and a diuretic and by getting up at night. The nurse teaches dangling, places a commode, uses fall precautions and monitors standing pressure and falls. Fluid restriction would worsen it. New antihypertensives plus night urination equals a fall waiting to happen.
questions.strategy: Tie each action to preventing a fall.

questions.topic: why this patient gets this drug
questions.stem: A patient taking lisinopril for 3 months has a dry, tickling cough with clear lungs and no fever. What should the nurse anticipate?
questions.objective: why this patient gets this drug

options.text: A cough suppressant and continuing the lisinopril
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Suppressing the cough leaves the cause in place.

options.text: A switch to losartan
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors block the breakdown of bradykinin, which builds up in the airway and causes a dry cough. An ARB lowers pressure through the same chain without the bradykinin buildup.

options.text: A chest x ray for pneumonia
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Clear lungs and no fever do not suggest pneumonia.

options.text: Stopping all blood pressure drugs
options.rationale: Absolute language The pressure still needs treatment.

questions.takeaway: ACE cough: switch to an ARB.
questions.strategy: Pick the change that removes the mechanism.

questions.stem: How do beta blockers lower blood pressure?

options.text: They block calcium entry into arterial smooth muscle, relaxing the arteries
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is how dipine calcium channel blockers work.

options.text: They block the enzyme that forms angiotensin II
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is how ACE inhibitors work.

options.text: They remove sodium and water through the kidneys
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is how diuretics work.

options.text: They block beta receptors, slowing the heart and reducing its force
options.rationale: Beta receptors on the heart respond to epinephrine and norepinephrine by speeding the rate and strengthening each beat. Blocking them slows the rate, reduces the force and slows conduction through the AV node. Less work also means less oxygen demand, which is why they help after MI and with angina.

questions.takeaway: Beta blocker = slower, softer heartbeat.
questions.strategy: Locate the drug's target: heart, vessels or volume.

questions.stem: Select all of the conditions for which a beta blocker is commonly used.

options.text: Hypertension after a myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Beta blockers lower oxygen demand after MI and in angina, slow conduction in atrial fibrillation and protect the heart long term in heart failure (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate).

options.text: Stable angina
options.rationale: Beta blockers lower oxygen demand after MI and in angina, slow conduction in atrial fibrillation and protect the heart long term in heart failure (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate).

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate
options.rationale: Beta blockers lower oxygen demand after MI and in angina, slow conduction in atrial fibrillation and protect the heart long term in heart failure (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate).

options.text: Acute asthma attack
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blocking beta 2 can tighten the airways; beta blockers are avoided in asthma.

options.text: Symptomatic bradycardia
options.rationale: Near miss concept A beta blocker would slow an already slow heart further.

options.text: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
options.rationale: Beta blockers lower oxygen demand after MI and in angina, slow conduction in atrial fibrillation and protect the heart long term in heart failure (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate).

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers: after MI, angina, rate control, heart failure.
questions.strategy: Ask what a slower, weaker heartbeat would do to this patient.

questions.stem: Match each beta blocker to its selectivity.
questions.takeaway: Beta 1 receptors are mainly in the heart (beta 1 = 1 heart). Beta 2 receptors are mainly in the lungs (beta 2 = 2 lungs). Metoprolol and atenolol mostly block beta 1. Propranolol and carvedilol block both. 1 heart, 2 lungs.
questions.strategy: Learn the two nonselective names and assume the rest are selective.

questions.stem: Why is propranolol avoided in a patient with asthma?

options.text: It suppresses the cough reflex and traps mucus
options.rationale: Near miss concept Propranolol does not suppress cough.

options.text: It causes a dry cough by raising bradykinin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bradykinin cough is an ACE inhibitor effect.

options.text: It blocks beta 2 receptors, which can tighten the airways
options.rationale: Beta 2 receptors relax the smooth muscle of the airways. Propranolol blocks them, so the airways can tighten into bronchospasm. A cardioselective drug such as metoprolol is preferred, still with caution because selectivity drops at higher doses.

options.text: It lowers potassium and weakens the muscles used for breathing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Beta blockers do not lower potassium.

questions.takeaway: Nonselective beta blocker plus asthma = bronchospasm risk.
questions.strategy: Map the receptor to the organ.

questions.stem: Select all of the adverse effects the nurse watches for with metoprolol.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.rationale: Slowing the heart can go too far, causing bradycardia, hypotension and fatigue. Beta blockers also blunt the fast heart rate and tremor that warn of hypoglycemia.

options.text: Hypotension
options.rationale: Slowing the heart can go too far, causing bradycardia, hypotension and fatigue. Beta blockers also blunt the fast heart rate and tremor that warn of hypoglycemia.

options.text: Fatigue
options.rationale: Slowing the heart can go too far, causing bradycardia, hypotension and fatigue. Beta blockers also blunt the fast heart rate and tremor that warn of hypoglycemia.

options.text: Persistent dry cough
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dry cough is an ACE inhibitor effect.

options.text: Masked signs of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Slowing the heart can go too far, causing bradycardia, hypotension and fatigue. Beta blockers also blunt the fast heart rate and tremor that warn of hypoglycemia.

options.text: Ankle edema
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ankle edema is a dipine calcium channel blocker effect.

questions.takeaway: Slow, low, tired, and hypoglycemia hidden.
questions.strategy: Each correct effect follows from slowing the heart or blocking epinephrine.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes takes metoprolol. Which sign of hypoglycemia is most likely to remain?

options.text: Rapid heart rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Beta blockade prevents the heart from speeding up.

options.text: Tremor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tremor is a beta response and is blunted.

options.text: Sweating
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia triggers epinephrine, which normally causes a fast heart rate, tremor and palpitations through beta receptors. Beta blockers blunt these. Sweating runs through a different nerve pathway, so it usually remains, and confusion still appears.

options.text: Palpitations
options.rationale: Near miss concept Palpitations come from the fast rate the drug blocks.

questions.takeaway: On a beta blocker, sweating and confusion may be the only clues.
questions.strategy: Remove every sign the beta receptor produces.

questions.stem: Which assessment is required right before giving a beta blocker?

options.text: Serum potassium and daily weight
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Potassium and weight matter for diuretics, not this dose.

options.text: Respiratory rate and pain level
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data These match opioids, not beta blockers.

options.text: Radial pulse for 15 seconds and an oral temperature
options.rationale: Near miss concept A 15 second radial count can miss irregular or slow beats.

options.text: Apical pulse for a full minute and blood pressure
options.rationale: Beta blockers slow the heart and drop the pressure, so you check both. Count the apical pulse for a full minute, because slow or irregular rhythms are easy to miscount over 15 seconds.

questions.takeaway: Apical pulse for a full minute plus blood pressure.
questions.strategy: Assess what the drug can push too low.

questions.stem: Where do the hold parameters for a beta blocker come from?

options.text: The drug reference, since orders never include them
options.rationale: Absolute language Orders often include parameters; never is false.

options.text: The order, which the nurse reads each time
options.rationale: Hold parameters are part of the order, such as hold for heart rate under 60 or systolic under 100. A heart rate under 60 is a common threshold, but you always read the order. If there is none and the findings worry you, you hold and clarify.

options.text: The nurse's judgment of a heart rate under 50
options.rationale: Near miss concept The common threshold is 60, and even that comes from the order.

options.text: Hospital policy, which applies the same number to every patient
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Parameters can differ by patient; the order governs.

questions.takeaway: Read the order every time. Often HR under 60.
questions.strategy: The order is the source; numbers you remember are a backup.

questions.stem: Why must a beta blocker not be stopped abruptly?

options.text: The blood pressure falls sharply when it stops
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stopping raises, not lowers, the rate and pressure.

options.text: Rebound tachycardia can trigger angina or MI
options.rationale: With long term use, the heart makes more beta receptors. If the drug stops suddenly, those receptors are flooded with epinephrine, causing rebound tachycardia, high pressure, angina and possibly MI. The provider tapers the dose.

options.text: Stopping causes an immediate allergic reaction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stopping a drug does not cause an allergy.

options.text: The drug builds up in the kidneys once it stops
options.rationale: Near miss concept A stopped drug clears; it does not build up.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers: taper, never stop suddenly.
questions.strategy: Think about the receptors left unblocked.

questions.stem: What makes carvedilol useful in heart failure?

options.text: It removes fluid like a loop diuretic
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not act as a diuretic.

options.text: It raises the heart rate to improve output
options.rationale: Near miss concept It slows the heart rate.

options.text: It is cardioselective and safe in asthma
options.rationale: Near miss concept Carvedilol is nonselective and is avoided in asthma.

options.text: It also relaxes vessels, lowering the heart's workload
options.rationale: Carvedilol blocks beta 1 and beta 2 and also alpha 1 receptors on vessels, so it slows the heart and relaxes vessels. That lowers the heart's workload and slows damage over time.

questions.takeaway: Carvedilol: beta blocker that also relaxes vessels, for heart failure.
questions.strategy: Look for the extra action.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about the two forms of metoprolol.
questions.sentence: Metoprolol [[1]] is short acting and is given twice daily. Metoprolol [[2]] is extended release, given once daily, and is the form used for [[3]].

tartrate
atenolol
succinate
tartrate
carvedilol
acute asthma

The two are not interchangeable mg for mg, and succinate is never crushed. Tartrate twice daily. Succinate once daily, heart failure, do not crush.
