questions.stem: Select all of the findings that make the nurse question a new beta blocker order.

options.text: Heart rate of 48
options.rationale: Beta blockers are questioned with bradycardia, heart block, asthma when the drug is nonselective, and acute decompensated heart failure, where reducing the force of the heart can worsen the failure. They are started in heart failure once the patient is stable.

options.text: Second degree heart block
options.rationale: Beta blockers are questioned with bradycardia, heart block, asthma when the drug is nonselective, and acute decompensated heart failure, where reducing the force of the heart can worsen the failure. They are started in heart failure once the patient is stable.

options.text: Asthma, with propranolol ordered
options.rationale: Beta blockers are questioned with bradycardia, heart block, asthma when the drug is nonselective, and acute decompensated heart failure, where reducing the force of the heart can worsen the failure. They are started in heart failure once the patient is stable.

options.text: Blood pressure of 142/88
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem High pressure is a reason to give it, not to question it.

options.text: Acute decompensated heart failure with crackles
options.rationale: Beta blockers are questioned with bradycardia, heart block, asthma when the drug is nonselective, and acute decompensated heart failure, where reducing the force of the heart can worsen the failure. They are started in heart failure once the patient is stable.

options.text: Stable angina
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Angina is an indication.

questions.takeaway: Slow, blocked, wheezing or acutely failing: question it.
questions.strategy: Find conditions the drug would make worse.

questions.stem: Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO BID is due at 0900. The apical pulse is 52, blood pressure is 98/58, and the patient says, "I get lightheaded when I stand up." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give half the dose and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is outside the nurse's scope.

options.text: Give it with food to reduce the dizziness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Food does not fix bradycardia and hypotension.

options.text: Give the dose, since metoprolol is ordered twice daily on schedule
options.rationale: Institution as rationale A scheduled order is not a reason to give a drug that is already acting too strongly.

options.text: Hold it, keep the patient in bed, and notify the provider
options.rationale: A slow rate, low pressure and dizziness on standing mean the drug effect is too strong. Hold the dose, recheck the apical pulse for a full minute, keep the patient in bed with the call light in reach, notify the provider and document.

questions.takeaway: Slow HR + low BP + dizziness = hold.
questions.strategy: Weigh the three findings together.

questions.stem: Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO BID is due. The order says hold for heart rate under 60. The apical pulse is 62, blood pressure is 124/78, and the patient walked to the bathroom without dizziness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recheck the pulse in 30 minutes before deciding
options.rationale: Correct but premature The findings are stable now; delaying a scheduled dose has no benefit.

options.text: Give the dose as ordered
options.rationale: The rate is above the hold parameter, the pressure is normal and there are no symptoms. The nurse gives it. Holding a safe dose has its own risk, because missed beta blocker doses allow rebound.

options.text: Hold the dose, since 62 is close to 60
options.rationale: Near miss concept The parameter is under 60; 62 does not meet it and the patient is well.

options.text: Notify the provider before giving it
options.rationale: Correct but premature Nothing here needs a provider decision.

questions.takeaway: Above the parameter and asymptomatic: give.
questions.strategy: Do not invent a reason to hold.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes taking metoprolol is found sweating and confused at 1500. The heart rate is 64. The patient denies feeling shaky. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the next metoprolol dose
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question The drug may hide symptoms, but holding it does not treat this episode.

options.text: Recheck the heart rate in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature A normal heart rate is expected on a beta blocker and does not rule out a low glucose.

options.text: Notify the provider of a possible stroke
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Confusion can mean stroke, but hypoglycemia is quick to check and fix.

options.text: Check the blood glucose
options.rationale: On a beta blocker the fast heart rate and tremor of hypoglycemia may be absent, leaving sweating and confusion. A fingerstick takes seconds and the treatment is fast.

questions.takeaway: Sweating and confusion on a beta blocker: check the glucose.
questions.strategy: Rule out the quick, fixable cause first.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma who uses an albuterol inhaler twice a week has a new order for propranolol for hypertension. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it and check the peak flow daily
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Monitoring catches harm after it starts.

options.text: Give it and keep albuterol at the bedside
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Having a rescue inhaler ready does not make a risky drug safe.

options.text: Give it, since the asthma is mild
options.rationale: Near miss concept Even mild asthma can tighten with beta 2 blockade.

options.text: Clarify the order before giving the first dose
options.rationale: Propranolol is nonselective and blocks the beta 2 receptors that keep airways open. The nurse clarifies. A cardioselective agent or another class is safer.

questions.takeaway: Asthma plus nonselective beta blocker: clarify.
questions.strategy: When the drug itself is the risk, clarify before giving.

questions.stem: A patient taking metoprolol for 2 years says, "I am going on vacation and do not want to bother refilling it, so I will just stop it for 2 weeks." Which response is best?

options.text: "That is fine for a short break; just restart it at the usual dose when you get home."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stopping suddenly causes rebound tachycardia.

options.text: "Take half a tablet while you are away to make it last."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is the provider's decision.

options.text: "Stopping suddenly can cause a fast heart rate or chest pain; let us arrange a refill."
options.rationale: After long term use, abrupt stopping causes rebound tachycardia, high pressure and possibly angina or MI. The nurse explains why and solves the real problem: the refill.

options.text: "Check your pulse daily while you are off it."
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Monitoring does not prevent the rebound.

questions.takeaway: Teach the danger, solve the barrier.
questions.strategy: Pick the response that addresses why the patient wants to stop.

questions.stem: A patient on metoprolol 100 mg PO BID was given an extra dose in error. One hour later the apical pulse is 44, blood pressure is 84/50, and the patient is dizzy and pale. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Recheck vital signs at the next routine check
Encourage walking to raise the heart rate
Give the next dose early to restore the schedule
Hold the next scheduled dose
Notify the provider
Hypoglycemia
Beta blocker toxicity with bradycardia
Bronchospasm
Rebound tachycardia
Heart rate and rhythm
Peak flow
Blood pressure
Serum potassium
Daily weight

questions.takeaway: An extra dose with a rate of 44, low pressure and dizziness is beta blocker toxicity. Hold the next dose, notify the provider, keep the patient safe in bed with frequent checks, not routine ones, and monitor heart rate, rhythm and pressure. The incident report follows once the patient is safe. Too much beta blocker: hold, notify, monitor rate and pressure.
questions.strategy: Choose actions and monitors that match what the drug does.

questions.stem: How does lisinopril lower blood pressure?

options.text: It blocks the enzyme that forms angiotensin II
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II. Lisinopril blocks the enzyme, so less angiotensin II forms. Vessels relax and less aldosterone is released, so less sodium and water are held.

options.text: It blocks calcium entry into the heart muscle
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is how diltiazem and verapamil work.

options.text: It blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is how spironolactone works.

options.text: It blocks the angiotensin II receptor on vessels
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is how ARBs such as losartan work.

questions.takeaway: pril blocks the enzyme.
questions.strategy: Trace the drug through the RAAS chain and ask what each blocked step causes.

questions.stem: Why do ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough?

options.text: They dry the airway lining by removing fluid from it
options.rationale: Near miss concept ACE inhibitors are not diuretics.

options.text: Bradykinin builds up because ACE also breaks it down
options.rationale: The same enzyme that makes angiotensin II also breaks down bradykinin. When ACE is blocked, bradykinin builds up in the airway and triggers a dry, persistent cough. ARBs do not affect bradykinin, so switching usually stops the cough.

options.text: They block beta 2 receptors in the airways
options.rationale: Near miss concept Beta 2 blockade is a nonselective beta blocker effect.

options.text: They raise potassium, which irritates the airway
options.rationale: Near miss concept High potassium affects muscle and heart, not cough.

questions.takeaway: ACE cough = bradykinin.
questions.strategy: Name the second job of the blocked enzyme.

questions.stem: Why can ACE inhibitors and ARBs raise the serum potassium?

options.text: Less aldosterone means the kidneys excrete less potassium
options.rationale: Aldosterone makes the kidneys hold sodium and get rid of potassium. With less aldosterone, potassium is kept. That is why you check potassium and avoid salt substitutes and supplements unless ordered.

options.text: They contain potassium in the tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tablets do not supply potassium.

options.text: They damage the kidneys in every patient
options.rationale: Absolute language Kidney injury can occur but not in every patient, and it is not the main reason.

options.text: They cause potassium to shift out of cells
options.rationale: Near miss concept The cause is less excretion, not a shift.

questions.takeaway: Less aldosterone, more potassium.
questions.strategy: Trace the drug through the RAAS chain and ask what each blocked step causes.

questions.stem: Select all of the adverse effects the nurse monitors for with lisinopril.

options.text: Dry cough
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors cause a bradykinin cough, high potassium, angioedema and first dose hypotension. The first dose can drop the pressure sharply, especially with a diuretic or volume depletion.

options.text: Hyperkalemia
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors cause a bradykinin cough, high potassium, angioedema and first dose hypotension. The first dose can drop the pressure sharply, especially with a diuretic or volume depletion.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lisinopril raises potassium; loops and thiazides lower it.

options.text: Angioedema
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors cause a bradykinin cough, high potassium, angioedema and first dose hypotension. The first dose can drop the pressure sharply, especially with a diuretic or volume depletion.

options.text: Hypotension after the first dose
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors cause a bradykinin cough, high potassium, angioedema and first dose hypotension. The first dose can drop the pressure sharply, especially with a diuretic or volume depletion.

options.text: Reflex tachycardia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reflex tachycardia goes with dipine calcium channel blockers.

questions.takeaway: Cough, potassium up, angioedema, first dose drop.
questions.strategy: Trace the drug through the RAAS chain and ask what each blocked step causes.

questions.stem: What is angioedema from an ACE inhibitor?

options.text: A cough that worsens at night
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes the bradykinin cough.

options.text: A raised rash on the trunk that fades within a day or two
options.rationale: Near miss concept A trunk rash is not angioedema.

options.text: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat that can block the airway
options.rationale: Angioedema is deep swelling of the face, lips, tongue and throat, also driven by bradykinin. It can occur after the first dose or after years. Throat swelling can close the airway, so it is an emergency.

options.text: Ankle swelling from fluid retention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ankle edema is a calcium channel blocker effect.

questions.takeaway: Lips or tongue swelling = airway emergency.
questions.strategy: Find the option that threatens the airway.

questions.stem: A patient on lisinopril develops swelling of the lips and tongue. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Document the reaction and add it to the allergy list
Assess the airway and call for help
Stop the lisinopril
Give emergency drugs per order and prepare airway equipment

questions.takeaway: Remove the cause, then protect the airway and bring help. Treatment follows per order, and the reaction is documented so the patient never gets an ACE inhibitor again. Stop, airway, help, treat, document.
questions.strategy: Exposure off, airway on, then paper.

questions.stem: Select all of the values the nurse monitors for a patient on an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

options.text: Blood glucose
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data These drugs do not change glucose.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Potassium rises with less aldosterone. Creatinine can rise as pressure inside the kidney's filters falls, especially early or in a dehydrated patient. Blood pressure is the target.

options.text: Apical pulse before each dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept They do not slow the heart; the apical pulse check belongs to beta blockers.

options.text: Serum creatinine
options.rationale: Potassium rises with less aldosterone. Creatinine can rise as pressure inside the kidney's filters falls, especially early or in a dehydrated patient. Blood pressure is the target.

options.text: Blood pressure
options.rationale: Potassium rises with less aldosterone. Creatinine can rise as pressure inside the kidney's filters falls, especially early or in a dehydrated patient. Blood pressure is the target.

options.text: Platelet count
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data They do not affect platelets.

questions.takeaway: Potassium, creatinine, blood pressure.
questions.strategy: Monitor what the chain controls.

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a patient starting lisinopril?

options.text: Take potassium supplements to prevent cramps
options.rationale: Near miss concept Supplements raise potassium further.

options.text: Use a salt substitute to cut down on sodium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride, which adds to the high potassium risk.

options.text: Avoid salt substitutes unless the provider approves
options.rationale: Salt substitutes replace sodium chloride with potassium chloride. On a drug that already holds potassium, they can push the level dangerously high.

options.text: Eat extra bananas and potatoes every day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Extra potassium foods are for loops and thiazides, not ACE inhibitors.

questions.takeaway: Salt substitute = potassium.
questions.strategy: Ask which direction the drug pushes potassium.

questions.stem: How does losartan differ from lisinopril?

options.text: It blocks ACE more strongly, so it works faster
options.rationale: Near miss concept Losartan does not block ACE at all.

options.text: It lowers potassium instead of raising it
options.rationale: Near miss concept ARBs also raise potassium.

options.text: It acts on the heart rate instead of on the blood vessels themselves
options.rationale: Near miss concept ARBs relax vessels; they do not slow the heart.

options.text: It blocks the angiotensin II receptor, so bradykinin does not build up
options.rationale: ARBs let angiotensin II form but block its receptor, so vessels relax and aldosterone falls. Because ACE still breaks down bradykinin, cough is rare. Potassium can still rise.

questions.takeaway: sartan: same effect, no bradykinin cough, potassium still rises.
questions.strategy: Trace the drug through the RAAS chain and ask what each blocked step causes.

questions.stem: A patient has orders for both lisinopril and valsartan. Why should the nurse clarify?

options.text: Valsartan inactivates lisinopril
options.rationale: Near miss concept They do not inactivate each other.

options.text: The combination causes bradycardia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Neither drug slows the heart.

options.text: They must be taken at different times of day to avoid an interaction between them
options.rationale: Near miss concept Timing does not make the combination safe.

options.text: Together they raise the risk of high potassium, hypotension and kidney injury
options.rationale: An ACE inhibitor and an ARB block the same chain twice. The combination raises the risk of high potassium, low pressure and kidney injury without enough added benefit, so they are not given together.

questions.takeaway: pril plus sartan: clarify.
questions.strategy: Two drugs on one target usually means double the harm.

questions.stem: Select all of the conditions for which an ACE inhibitor or ARB is a good choice.

options.text: Hypertension with diabetes
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs protect the kidneys in diabetes and kidney disease, lower the heart's workload in heart failure and protect the heart after MI.

options.text: Chronic kidney disease with protein in the urine
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs protect the kidneys in diabetes and kidney disease, lower the heart's workload in heart failure and protect the heart after MI.

options.text: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs protect the kidneys in diabetes and kidney disease, lower the heart's workload in heart failure and protect the heart after MI.

options.text: Hyperkalemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept These drugs raise potassium.

options.text: After a myocardial infarction
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs protect the kidneys in diabetes and kidney disease, lower the heart's workload in heart failure and protect the heart after MI.

options.text: Previous angioedema from lisinopril
options.rationale: Near miss concept A history of ACE inhibitor angioedema is a reason to avoid this class or use great caution.

questions.takeaway: Kidneys, failing heart, after MI.
questions.strategy: Trace the drug through the RAAS chain and ask what each blocked step causes.

questions.stem: Why is the first dose of an ACE inhibitor a fall risk?

options.text: It lowers the blood glucose
options.rationale: Near miss concept They do not affect glucose.

options.text: It causes sedation
options.rationale: Near miss concept These drugs are not sedating.

options.text: It can drop the pressure sharply, especially with a diuretic
options.rationale: A patient whose RAAS is very active, such as one on a diuretic or one who is dehydrated, depends on angiotensin II to hold the pressure up. The first dose can drop it suddenly, so you check pressure and use orthostatic precautions.

options.text: It causes bradycardia within an hour of the first dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept They do not slow the heart.

questions.takeaway: First dose: watch the pressure and prevent falls.
questions.strategy: Ask who depends most on the blocked hormone.

questions.stem: A patient who has taken lisinopril for 4 years reports that the lips feel tight. The nurse sees swelling of the lips and tongue, and the voice sounds muffled. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Stop the drug, assess the airway and call for help
options.rationale: Swelling with a muffled voice means the airway is involved. The nurse stops the drug, protects the airway and calls for help. Angioedema can occur at any time, not only after the first dose.

options.text: Document a new allergy in the record
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting comes after the airway is secure.

options.text: Reassure the patient, since the drug has been taken for years
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Angioedema can appear after years of use.

options.text: Give an antihistamine and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting an hour with a changing voice is unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Years on the drug does not rule out angioedema.
questions.strategy: Airway first.

questions.stem: Lisinopril 20 mg PO daily is due. Morning labs show potassium 5.9 mEq/L and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, up from 1.1 last week. Blood pressure is 128/76. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold it and notify the provider of the labs
options.rationale: A potassium of 5.9 is above the 3.5 to 5.0 range, and the rising creatinine means the kidneys are clearing less. Lisinopril makes both worse. The nurse holds and notifies.

options.text: Give it and encourage more fluids
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Fluids do not fix hyperkalemia and the drug still raises potassium.

options.text: Give it and recheck the labs tomorrow
options.rationale: Correct but premature A potassium of 5.9 needs action now.

options.text: Give it, since the blood pressure is well controlled today
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Good pressure control does not cancel a dangerous potassium.

questions.takeaway: High potassium plus rising creatinine: hold and notify.
questions.strategy: Check what the drug does to the abnormal lab.

questions.stem: A patient taking losartan says, "I switched to a salt substitute and use it on everything now." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Teach that most salt substitutes are potassium and should be avoided
options.rationale: Salt substitutes are usually potassium chloride. With an ARB holding potassium, heavy use can push the level dangerously high. The nurse teaches other ways to flavor food, such as herbs, and checks the potassium.

options.text: Suggest using it only at dinner
options.rationale: Near miss concept Less of a potassium product is still a potassium product.

options.text: Tell the patient to drink more water with meals when using it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Water does not prevent hyperkalemia.

options.text: Praise the patient for lowering sodium
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Praise reinforces a risky habit.

questions.takeaway: On a pril or sartan, no salt substitutes.
questions.strategy: Spot the hidden potassium.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure takes lisinopril and spironolactone and recently started a potassium supplement for leg cramps. The patient reports weakness. Potassium is 6.3 mEq/L and the monitor shows peaked T waves. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Encourage bananas and orange juice
Hold the potassium supplement and notify the provider
Give the morning spironolactone dose
Place the patient on continuous cardiac monitoring
Increase the supplement to treat the cramps
Hypokalemia
Dehydration
Hyperkalemia from potassium retaining drugs
Digoxin toxicity
Cardiac rhythm
Blood glucose
Serum calcium
Peak flow
Serum potassium

questions.takeaway: An ACE inhibitor and spironolactone both hold potassium, and a supplement adds more. A level of 6.3 with peaked T waves threatens the heart. The nurse holds the supplement and the potassium retaining drugs, notifies the provider, monitors the rhythm and trends the potassium. pril plus spironolactone plus supplement = hyperkalemia.
questions.strategy: Add up every source of potassium.

questions.stem: An 80 year old on furosemide receives the first dose of lisinopril at 0900. Which nursing action is most important afterward?

options.text: Check blood pressure and help the patient up the first time
options.rationale: A patient on a diuretic depends on angiotensin II to hold the pressure up, so the first ACE inhibitor dose can drop it sharply. The nurse checks pressure and assists with the first time up.

options.text: Check the apical pulse before lunch
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lisinopril does not slow the heart; the pressure is the concern.

options.text: Check the blood glucose at noon
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Glucose is not affected.

options.text: Encourage walking in the hall right after the first dose is given
options.rationale: Near miss concept Unassisted walking risks a fall during first dose hypotension.

questions.takeaway: First dose plus diuretic: watch the pressure, assist up.
questions.strategy: Prevent the predictable fall.

questions.stem: How does amlodipine lower blood pressure?

options.text: It blocks calcium entry into arterial muscle, relaxing arteries
options.rationale: Arterial smooth muscle needs calcium to contract. Amlodipine blocks calcium channels in the artery wall, so arteries relax and resistance falls. It has little effect on heart rate.

options.text: It blocks the angiotensin II receptor
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is an ARB.

options.text: It slows the heart rate and AV conduction
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes diltiazem and verapamil.

options.text: It removes sodium and water at the distal tubule
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a thiazide.

questions.takeaway: dipine relaxes arteries.
questions.strategy: First decide whether the drug acts on the vessels or the heart.

questions.stem: Match each statement to the calcium channel blocker group it describes.

rows.text: Used to control the rate in atrial fibrillation
Can cause reflex tachycardia and flushing
Check the heart rate before giving

questions.takeaway: Dipines relax arteries, so the pressure falls and the heart may speed up by reflex, with flushing, headache and ankle edema. Diltiazem and verapamil act on the heart, slowing rate and conduction, so you check the heart rate first. Verapamil also slows the gut and causes constipation. dipine = vessels. diltiazem and verapamil = heart.
questions.strategy: First decide whether the drug acts on the vessels or the heart.

questions.stem: Select all of the adverse effects of amlodipine.

options.text: Ankle edema
options.rationale: Relaxing arteries drops the pressure (dizziness), widens vessels in the head and skin (headache, flushing) and raises pressure in the small vessels of the legs (ankle edema).

options.text: Headache
options.rationale: Relaxing arteries drops the pressure (dizziness), widens vessels in the head and skin (headache, flushing) and raises pressure in the small vessels of the legs (ankle edema).

options.text: Hyperkalemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept High potassium is an effect of ACE inhibitors, ARBs and spironolactone.

options.text: Dizziness
options.rationale: Relaxing arteries drops the pressure (dizziness), widens vessels in the head and skin (headache, flushing) and raises pressure in the small vessels of the legs (ankle edema).

options.text: Flushing
options.rationale: Relaxing arteries drops the pressure (dizziness), widens vessels in the head and skin (headache, flushing) and raises pressure in the small vessels of the legs (ankle edema).

options.text: Dry cough
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dry cough is an ACE inhibitor effect.

questions.takeaway: dipine: dizzy, flushed, headache, swollen ankles.
questions.strategy: Every correct effect comes from wider arteries.

questions.stem: Why does amlodipine cause ankle edema?

options.text: It weakens the heart and causes heart failure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Amlodipine does not weaken the heart.

options.text: It lowers albumin made by the liver
options.rationale: Near miss concept It has no effect on albumin.

options.text: It causes the kidneys to hold sodium and water
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is not volume retention, which is why diuretics help little.

options.text: Widened arterioles raise pressure in the leg capillaries
options.rationale: Amlodipine opens the arterioles more than the veins, so more pressure reaches the leg capillaries and fluid leaks into the tissue. It is not fluid overload. The patient reports it, and the provider may lower the dose or change the drug.

questions.takeaway: dipine edema is local, not overload.
questions.strategy: Separate local leakage from total body fluid.

questions.stem: Which assessment must the nurse complete before giving diltiazem?

options.text: Heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: Diltiazem slows the heart rate and AV conduction and also lowers pressure. You check both before the dose and hold per the order parameters.

options.text: Serum potassium and creatinine levels
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data These matter for ACE inhibitors, ARBs and spironolactone.

options.text: Blood glucose and weight
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Diltiazem does not affect glucose.

options.text: Respiratory rate and sedation
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data These match opioids.

questions.takeaway: Diltiazem: heart rate first.
questions.strategy: First decide whether the drug acts on the vessels or the heart.

questions.stem: Why is diltiazem used in atrial fibrillation?

options.text: It prevents clots in the atria
options.rationale: Near miss concept Anticoagulants prevent clots.

options.text: It strengthens each contraction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diltiazem reduces the force of contraction.

options.text: It converts the rhythm back to normal sinus rhythm within hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rate control drugs slow the ventricles; they do not restore normal rhythm.

options.text: It slows conduction through the AV node, controlling the rate
options.rationale: In atrial fibrillation the atria fire chaotically, and the AV node passes many impulses to the ventricles. Diltiazem slows conduction through the AV node, so fewer impulses get through and the ventricular rate falls.

questions.takeaway: Rate control: beta blocker or diltiazem.
questions.strategy: Ask what controls the rate, not the rhythm.

questions.stem: A patient is starting verapamil. Which adverse effect should the nurse teach about?

options.text: Dry cough
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cough is an ACE inhibitor effect.

options.text: Ankle edema with flushing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Edema and flushing are more typical of dipines.

options.text: High potassium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Verapamil does not raise potassium.

options.text: Constipation
options.rationale: Verapamil slows smooth muscle in the gut as well as the heart, so constipation is common. Teach fluids, fiber and activity, and to report it.

questions.takeaway: Verapamil: constipation.
questions.strategy: Remember the one gut effect in this group.

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking nifedipine XL?

options.text: Avoid grapefruit juice, which raises drug levels
options.rationale: Grapefruit blocks the gut enzyme that breaks down several calcium channel blockers, so levels rise and the pressure can fall too far. XL tablets are swallowed whole.

options.text: Take it only when blood pressure is high
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blood pressure needs daily control.

options.text: Expect a heart rate below 50 as a normal effect
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nifedipine tends to raise, not lower, the heart rate.

options.text: Crush it if it is hard to swallow
options.rationale: Near miss concept XL is extended release and must not be crushed.

questions.takeaway: Calcium channel blockers: no grapefruit, do not crush XL.
questions.strategy: Look for the interaction and the form.

questions.stem: Why does the nurse watch closely when diltiazem and metoprolol are given together?

options.text: Both cause severe ankle edema
options.rationale: Near miss concept Edema is a dipine effect.

options.text: Both raise potassium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Neither raises potassium.

options.text: Both slow the heart, so bradycardia or heart block can occur
options.rationale: Diltiazem and beta blockers both slow the heart rate and AV conduction. Together they can cause severe bradycardia, heart block and hypotension.

options.text: They cancel each other's effects, so neither one lowers the pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept They add together; they do not cancel.

questions.takeaway: Heart acting CCB plus beta blocker = double slowing.
questions.strategy: Add effects that point the same way.

questions.stem: A patient taking amlodipine 10 mg daily for 3 weeks has 1+ ankle edema in both legs. Lungs are clear, weight is unchanged, and the patient has no dyspnea. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Request a loop diuretic for the fluid overload
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Edema here is not overload; weight and lungs are stable, and diuretics help little.

options.text: Report the edema as a likely drug effect
options.rationale: Edema with clear lungs and stable weight in a patient on amlodipine points to the drug, not heart failure. The nurse reports it so the provider can lower the dose or switch.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1 liter a day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fluid restriction will not fix leakage from dilated arterioles.

options.text: Tell the patient to stop the amlodipine
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Stopping the drug is the provider's decision.

questions.takeaway: Swollen ankles plus stable weight on a dipine: drug effect.
questions.strategy: Check weight and lungs before calling it overload.

questions.stem: Diltiazem 60 mg PO is due for a patient with atrial fibrillation. The order says hold for heart rate under 60. The apical rate is 54 and irregular, and blood pressure is 104/62. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold it, notify the provider and document
options.rationale: A rate under the parameter means the drug is already slowing the heart enough. The nurse holds, notifies and documents.

options.text: Give it, since a radial count would read lower
options.rationale: Near miss concept An apical count is the accurate one.

options.text: Give half and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is not the nurse's decision.

options.text: Give it, since atrial fibrillation needs rate control
options.rationale: Institution as rationale The order parameter applies even when the drug is needed.

questions.takeaway: Under the parameter: hold.
questions.strategy: Read the parameter against the apical count.

questions.stem: A patient taking metoprolol 50 mg BID has a new order for diltiazem. The heart rate is 58 and the patient reports feeling tired and lightheaded. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the first diltiazem dose and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Giving a second rate slowing drug to a slow, symptomatic heart risks harm.

options.text: Clarify the new order with the provider before giving it
options.rationale: Diltiazem would add to the slowing from metoprolol in a patient who is already slow and symptomatic. The nurse clarifies before giving it.

options.text: Hold the metoprolol and give the diltiazem
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Choosing which drug to hold is the provider's call.

options.text: Give both and keep the patient in bed
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Bed rest manages a fall risk but not the bradycardia.

questions.takeaway: Two heart slowing drugs plus symptoms: clarify.
questions.strategy: When the order adds to a problem, clarify.

questions.stem: An 84 year old started verapamil 2 weeks ago and reports hard stools every 4 days and straining. Which response is best?

options.text: "Stop the verapamil until your bowels move."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The patient should not stop the drug without the provider.

options.text: "Take a laxative every day from now on."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Daily laxatives are not a nursing order.

options.text: "Constipation is a normal part of aging, so there is nothing we need to do about it."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It dismisses a treatable drug effect.

options.text: "This can come from verapamil; add fluid and fiber and let us tell your provider."
options.rationale: Verapamil slows gut smooth muscle. The nurse links the symptom to the drug, teaches fluid, fiber and activity and reports it.

questions.takeaway: New constipation on verapamil: drug effect.
questions.strategy: Connect the new symptom to the new drug.

questions.stem: Match each statement to the diuretic it describes.

rows.text: Strongest diuretic, works in the loop of Henle
Can raise glucose and uric acid
Still works when kidney function is low
First line for long term hypertension

questions.takeaway: Loops act in the loop of Henle, are strongest and still work with low kidney function. Thiazides act in the distal tubule, are moderate and are a first line for hypertension, and they raise glucose and uric acid. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct and keeps potassium. Loop strong, thiazide steady, spironolactone keeps potassium.
questions.strategy: Ask where in the nephron the drug works and which way it moves potassium.

questions.stem: Which patient is the best match for furosemide?

options.text: A patient with hyperkalemia and gout
options.rationale: Near miss concept Furosemide can raise uric acid; it is chosen for fluid overload.

options.text: A patient with new mild hypertension and normal kidneys
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mild hypertension starts with a thiazide or another first line drug.

options.text: A patient with pulmonary edema from heart failure
options.rationale: Furosemide is the strongest diuretic and works fast, so it is the drug for fluid overload such as pulmonary edema. It also works when kidney function is reduced, unlike a thiazide.

options.text: A patient with hypokalemia who needs a diuretic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Furosemide would push potassium lower.

questions.takeaway: Fluid overload: loop.
questions.strategy: Ask where in the nephron the drug works and which way it moves potassium.

questions.stem: Select all of the adverse effects of furosemide.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: Furosemide removes sodium, water, potassium and magnesium, causing low potassium, low magnesium, low pressure and dehydration. A fast IV push can damage the inner ear.

options.text: Hypotension
options.rationale: Furosemide removes sodium, water, potassium and magnesium, causing low potassium, low magnesium, low pressure and dehydration. A fast IV push can damage the inner ear.

options.text: Hearing damage with a fast IV push
options.rationale: Furosemide removes sodium, water, potassium and magnesium, causing low potassium, low magnesium, low pressure and dehydration. A fast IV push can damage the inner ear.

options.text: Hyperkalemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Furosemide lowers potassium; spironolactone raises it.

options.text: Hypomagnesemia
options.rationale: Furosemide removes sodium, water, potassium and magnesium, causing low potassium, low magnesium, low pressure and dehydration. A fast IV push can damage the inner ear.

options.text: Breast tissue enlargement
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a spironolactone effect.

questions.takeaway: Loop: low potassium, low magnesium, low pressure, ears.
questions.strategy: Ask where in the nephron the drug works and which way it moves potassium.

questions.stem: How does the nurse prevent hearing damage when giving IV furosemide?

options.text: Mix it with potassium chloride
options.rationale: Near miss concept Potassium chloride is never mixed in for a push.

options.text: Give it with food or milk to protect the ear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Food has nothing to do with an IV drug.

options.text: Push it slowly at the rate in the drug guide
options.rationale: High peak levels injure the inner ear. Pushing slowly keeps the peak lower. Risk rises with high doses, kidney impairment and other ototoxic drugs. Report ringing or hearing loss.

options.text: Give it only at bedtime
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diuretics are given in the morning, and timing does not protect hearing.

questions.takeaway: IV furosemide: push slowly, ask about ringing.
questions.strategy: Fast push, high peak, ear injury.

questions.stem: Select all of the effects of hydrochlorothiazide.

options.text: Lowers potassium
options.rationale: Thiazides lower potassium and sodium, and raise glucose, uric acid and calcium. Watch glucose in patients with diabetes and joint pain in patients with gout.

options.text: Raises blood glucose
options.rationale: Thiazides lower potassium and sodium, and raise glucose, uric acid and calcium. Watch glucose in patients with diabetes and joint pain in patients with gout.

options.text: Raises uric acid
options.rationale: Thiazides lower potassium and sodium, and raise glucose, uric acid and calcium. Watch glucose in patients with diabetes and joint pain in patients with gout.

options.text: Lowers calcium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thiazides raise calcium, which is the opposite of loops.

options.text: Lowers sodium
options.rationale: Thiazides lower potassium and sodium, and raise glucose, uric acid and calcium. Watch glucose in patients with diabetes and joint pain in patients with gout.

options.text: Raises magnesium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thiazides lower magnesium.

questions.takeaway: Thiazide: potassium and sodium down; glucose, uric acid, calcium up.
questions.strategy: Learn the three things that go up.

questions.stem: Why is a thiazide a poor choice when kidney function is very low?

options.text: It becomes toxic to the liver when the kidneys fail
options.rationale: Near miss concept Liver toxicity is not the concern.

options.text: It loses much of its effect when filtration is low
options.rationale: Thiazides need enough filtration to reach their site in the distal tubule. When kidney function is very low they lose much of their effect, and a loop diuretic is used instead.

options.text: It causes hyperkalemia in kidney disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thiazides lower potassium.

options.text: It cannot be absorbed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Absorption is not the problem.

questions.takeaway: Poor kidney function: loop, not thiazide.
questions.strategy: Match the drug's strength to the kidney's ability.

questions.stem: How does spironolactone work?

options.text: It blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct
options.rationale: Aldosterone makes the collecting duct keep sodium and get rid of potassium. Spironolactone blocks it, so a little sodium and water are lost and potassium is kept. It is a weak diuretic but protects the heart in heart failure.

options.text: It blocks the angiotensin II receptor
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is an ARB.

options.text: It draws water into the tubule by osmosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is mannitol.

options.text: It blocks sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is furosemide.

questions.takeaway: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone, keeps potassium.
questions.strategy: Ask where in the nephron the drug works and which way it moves potassium.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is specific to spironolactone among the diuretics?

options.text: Breast tissue enlargement
options.rationale: Spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors, which can cause breast tissue enlargement (gynecomastia). Its main danger is hyperkalemia.

options.text: Hearing damage
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hearing damage goes with loops.

options.text: High blood glucose
options.rationale: Near miss concept High glucose goes with thiazides.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spironolactone raises potassium.

questions.takeaway: Spironolactone: high potassium, breast tissue enlargement.
questions.strategy: Find the effect only one drug has.

questions.stem: Select all of the nursing actions that apply to every diuretic.

options.text: Give it in the morning
options.rationale: Morning dosing prevents nighttime urination. Daily weight and strict intake and output show the fluid change. Potassium is kept within 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

options.text: Weigh daily on the same scale at the same time
options.rationale: Morning dosing prevents nighttime urination. Daily weight and strict intake and output show the fluid change. Potassium is kept within 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

options.text: Keep strict intake and output
options.rationale: Morning dosing prevents nighttime urination. Daily weight and strict intake and output show the fluid change. Potassium is kept within 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

options.text: Give it at bedtime so it works overnight
options.rationale: Near miss concept A bedtime dose causes urination all night and falls.

options.text: Monitor serum potassium
options.rationale: Morning dosing prevents nighttime urination. Daily weight and strict intake and output show the fluid change. Potassium is kept within 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

options.text: Restrict all oral fluids
options.rationale: Absolute language Fluid restriction is a separate order; it is not part of every diuretic.

questions.takeaway: Morning, weight, intake and output, potassium.
questions.strategy: Pick what applies to the whole class.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about monitoring a patient with heart failure on a diuretic.
questions.sentence: The patient reports a weight gain of [[1]] in a day or [[2]] in a week. The normal serum potassium is [[3]].

options.text: 2 to 3 lb
5 lb
10 lb
2 to 3 lb
