2.5 to 3.5 mEq/L
3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L
5.0 to 6.5 mEq/L

questions.takeaway: A gain of 2 to 3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week is retained fluid, not tissue. Reporting it early lets the provider adjust the diuretic before the lungs fill. Potassium runs 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L. 2 to 3 lb a day, 5 lb a week, potassium 3.5 to 5.0.
questions.strategy: Weight change over a day is fluid.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about potassium on a loop diuretic.
questions.sentence: A potassium of 2.9 mEq/L causes [[1]], and the ECG may show [[2]]. The nurse teaches the patient to eat foods such as [[3]].

options.text: muscle weakness and cramps
tingling of the lips
bone pain
peaked T waves
a widened QRS only
flat T waves and U waves
cheese and crackers
bananas, potatoes and spinach
white rice and bread

questions.takeaway: Low potassium weakens muscle and causes cramps, and the ECG shows flat T waves and U waves with a risk of dysrhythmias. Peaked T waves go with high potassium. Bananas, potatoes, spinach and oranges are high in potassium. Low potassium: weak, cramping, flat T, U waves.
questions.strategy: Do not mix up the high and low potassium ECG.

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking spironolactone alone?

options.text: Expect your potassium to drop
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spironolactone raises potassium.

options.text: Take it at bedtime
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diuretics go in the morning.

options.text: Eat extra bananas and oranges every day with meals
options.rationale: Near miss concept Extra potassium foods are for loops and thiazides.

options.text: Avoid salt substitutes and potassium supplements unless ordered
options.rationale: Spironolactone keeps potassium. Salt substitutes are potassium chloride, and supplements add more, so both are avoided unless the provider orders them.

questions.takeaway: Spironolactone: no salt substitutes.
questions.strategy: Ask which way the drug moves potassium.

questions.stem: Furosemide 40 mg IV is due for a patient with heart failure. Potassium this morning is 3.1 mEq/L. The patient reports leg cramps. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give half the dose
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is the provider's decision.

options.text: Give it, since the patient still needs extra fluid removed
options.rationale: Institution as rationale The need for diuresis does not make a low potassium safe.

options.text: Hold it and notify the provider of the potassium
options.rationale: Furosemide will push a low potassium lower, raising the risk of dysrhythmias. The nurse holds and notifies so the potassium can be replaced first.

options.text: Give it with a banana
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Food cannot correct a potassium of 3.1 before an IV loop dose.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium before a loop: hold and notify.
questions.strategy: Check which way the drug moves the abnormal lab.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure on furosemide gained 3 lb since yesterday and has new crackles in both bases. SpO2 is 92% on room air. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and notify the provider
options.rationale: A 3 lb gain overnight with new crackles is fluid backing into the lungs. The nurse positions the patient upright to ease breathing and notifies the provider, who will likely adjust the diuretic.

options.text: Document the weight gain and recheck it tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting a sign of worsening failure without acting delays care.

options.text: Encourage more oral fluids to help thin the secretions in the lungs
options.rationale: Near miss concept More fluid worsens overload.

options.text: Reweigh after breakfast
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weighing after a meal adds food weight and wastes time.

questions.takeaway: Weight up plus crackles: position and notify.
questions.strategy: Act on the respiratory finding.

questions.stem: An 83 year old on furosemide 40 mg BID has a blood pressure of 88/54, a heart rate of 112, dry mucous membranes and dark urine. Weight is down 4 lb in 2 days. The 1700 dose is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it and recheck the blood pressure in 4 hours
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting 4 hours after more diuresis risks shock and a fall.

options.text: Give it, since the patient has heart failure
options.rationale: Institution as rationale The diagnosis does not override signs of dehydration.

options.text: Hold it and notify the provider of the volume loss
options.rationale: Low pressure, fast heart rate, dry mouth, dark urine and rapid weight loss mean too much fluid has been removed. Another dose would worsen it. The nurse holds and notifies.

options.text: Give it and encourage fluids
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Giving the diuretic while replacing fluid makes no sense.

questions.takeaway: Overdiuresis: hold and notify.
questions.strategy: The cues together outweigh the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes started hydrochlorothiazide 2 months ago. Fasting glucose has risen from 118 to 156 mg/dL. Diet and other drugs are unchanged. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to stop the thiazide
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Stopping the drug is the provider's decision.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 6 months
options.rationale: Correct but premature A clear rise needs reporting now.

options.text: Report the rise as a possible drug effect
options.rationale: Thiazides can raise blood glucose. A new rise with no other change points to the drug, and the provider may adjust the plan.

options.text: Teach the patient to cut carbohydrates further at each meal
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Diet teaching may help, but it misses the likely cause.

questions.takeaway: New glucose rise on a thiazide: report it.
questions.strategy: Link the new lab change to the new drug.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure takes spironolactone and lisinopril. This morning's potassium is 5.7 mEq/L. Spironolactone is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it, since it protects the heart
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Long term benefit does not outweigh an unsafe potassium now.

options.text: Hold it and notify the provider
options.rationale: Spironolactone and lisinopril both hold potassium. At 5.7, another dose raises the risk of dysrhythmias. The nurse holds and notifies.

options.text: Give it and recheck the potassium tomorrow
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting a day with a potassium of 5.7 is unsafe.

options.text: Give it with extra fluids
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fluids do not correct hyperkalemia.

questions.takeaway: High potassium on spironolactone: hold and notify.
questions.strategy: Add the potassium effects of every drug.

questions.stem: A patient on furosemide 80 mg IV BID for 3 days reports weakness and leg cramps. Potassium is 2.8 mEq/L, magnesium is 1.4 mg/dL, and the monitor shows flat T waves with U waves. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Give the next furosemide dose on time
Hold the furosemide and notify the provider
Encourage high sodium foods
Place the patient on continuous cardiac monitoring
Restrict oral intake
Hypokalemia from loop diuresis
Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypoglycemia
Blood glucose
Platelet count
Serum potassium
Serum calcium
Serum magnesium

questions.takeaway: Low potassium with flat T waves and U waves after high dose furosemide is diuretic hypokalemia, and low magnesium makes it harder to correct. The nurse holds the furosemide, notifies, monitors the rhythm and trends potassium and magnesium. Loop plus weakness plus U waves = low potassium; check magnesium too.
questions.strategy: Pick the monitors that match the cause.

questions.stem: What causes angina in coronary artery disease?

options.text: Inflammation of the sac around the heart
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is pericarditis.

options.text: Heart muscle demand for oxygen exceeds the supply through narrowed arteries
options.rationale: Plaque narrows the coronary arteries. At rest the flow may be enough, but exertion raises the heart's demand for oxygen, and the narrowed artery cannot keep up. The muscle becomes ischemic and hurts. Every CAD drug either raises supply, lowers demand or prevents a clot.

options.text: A clot that has fully blocked a coronary artery and killed muscle
options.rationale: Near miss concept Full blockage with muscle death is a myocardial infarction, not angina.

options.text: Spasm of the esophagus that mimics heart pain in most patients
options.rationale: Near miss concept Esophageal spasm can mimic angina but is not its cause.

questions.takeaway: Angina = demand over supply.
questions.strategy: Supply and demand frames every CAD drug.

questions.stem: Match each drug to its goal in coronary artery disease.
questions.takeaway: Nitroglycerin relieves pain now. Aspirin and clopidogrel keep platelets from clumping on plaque. Beta blockers slow the heart so it needs less oxygen. Statins lower LDL and make plaque less likely to rupture. ACE inhibitors or ARBs protect the heart after MI. Pain now, clot prevention, demand down, plaque steady.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the drug treats pain now or prevents the next event.

questions.stem: How does nitroglycerin relieve angina?

options.text: It dilates veins and coronary arteries, lowering demand and raising supply
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin mainly dilates veins, so less blood returns to the heart and it works less (lower preload, lower demand). It also dilates the coronary arteries, raising supply.

options.text: It slows the heart rate so the heart needs less oxygen
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is how beta blockers help; nitrates can raise the heart rate.

options.text: It thins the blood so it flows more easily through the plaque
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nitrates have no effect on clotting.

options.text: It dissolves the clot in the coronary artery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thrombolytics dissolve clots; nitrates do not.

questions.takeaway: Nitroglycerin: veins open, workload down.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the drug treats pain now or prevents the next event.

questions.stem: Place the steps for using sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain in order.

options.text: Call 911 if the pain is not better 5 minutes after the first tablet
Sit or lie down
Take a second tablet if needed, up to 3 total, 5 minutes apart
Place 1 tablet under the tongue and let it dissolve

questions.takeaway: Sitting prevents a fall from the drop in pressure. One tablet dissolves under the tongue. If the pain is not better 5 minutes after the first, the patient calls 911 then, without waiting for the third tablet, because unrelieved pain may be an MI. Up to 3 tablets may be taken 5 minutes apart. Sit, 1 tablet, 5 minutes, call 911 if not better.
questions.strategy: The 911 call comes after the first tablet, not the third.

questions.stem: Select all of the expected adverse effects of nitroglycerin.

options.text: Headache
options.rationale: Dilated vessels in the head cause headache and flushing, and dilated veins drop the pressure, causing dizziness. Headache is common and is not a reason to stop; acetaminophen often helps.

options.text: Hypotension
options.rationale: Dilated vessels in the head cause headache and flushing, and dilated veins drop the pressure, causing dizziness. Headache is common and is not a reason to stop; acetaminophen often helps.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nitrates often raise the heart rate by reflex.

options.text: Dizziness
options.rationale: Dilated vessels in the head cause headache and flushing, and dilated veins drop the pressure, causing dizziness. Headache is common and is not a reason to stop; acetaminophen often helps.

options.text: Flushing
options.rationale: Dilated vessels in the head cause headache and flushing, and dilated veins drop the pressure, causing dizziness. Headache is common and is not a reason to stop; acetaminophen often helps.

options.text: Hyperkalemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nitrates do not affect potassium.

questions.takeaway: Nitro: headache, low pressure, dizzy, flushed.
questions.strategy: Every correct effect comes from wider vessels.

questions.stem: When should the nurse hold sublingual nitroglycerin?

options.text: When the heart rate is over 90
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fast rate is not the hold rule for nitrates.

options.text: When the chest pain is rated under 5 of 10
options.rationale: Near miss concept Any ischemic chest pain is treated.

options.text: When the patient reports a headache
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Headache is expected and not a reason to hold.

options.text: When the systolic pressure is under 90 or per order
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin lowers the pressure. If the systolic is already under 90, another drop can cut blood flow to the heart and brain. Check pressure before every dose.

questions.takeaway: Nitro: check BP first, hold under 90 systolic.
questions.strategy: Assess what the drug lowers.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain took sildenafil 12 hours ago. Why is this important before nitroglycerin?

options.text: Together they can cause severe, dangerous hypotension
options.rationale: Sildenafil and tadalafil also dilate vessels through the same pathway. With a nitrate, the pressure can fall to a dangerous level. Always ask about these drugs before giving a nitrate and tell the provider.

options.text: Sildenafil causes bradycardia with nitrates
options.rationale: Near miss concept The danger is low pressure, not a slow rate.

options.text: It does not matter if more than 6 hours have passed
options.rationale: Near miss concept The interaction lasts at least 24 hours, longer with tadalafil.

options.text: Sildenafil blocks the effect of nitroglycerin
options.rationale: Near miss concept The problem is too much effect, not too little.

questions.takeaway: Nitrate plus sildenafil or tadalafil = severe hypotension.
questions.strategy: Look for two drugs that push the same way.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct teaching points for nitroglycerin.

options.text: Keep sublingual tablets in the original dark glass bottle
options.rationale: Light, heat and air weaken the tablets, so they stay in the dark glass bottle. A daily nitrate free period, often overnight, prevents tolerance. Gloves keep the nurse from absorbing the drug. Sitting prevents a fall.

options.text: Remove the patch for the ordered nitrate free period
options.rationale: Light, heat and air weaken the tablets, so they stay in the dark glass bottle. A daily nitrate free period, often overnight, prevents tolerance. Gloves keep the nurse from absorbing the drug. Sitting prevents a fall.

options.text: Apply the new patch to the same spot each time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rotate sites to prevent skin irritation.

options.text: Wear gloves when handling ointment or patches
options.rationale: Light, heat and air weaken the tablets, so they stay in the dark glass bottle. A daily nitrate free period, often overnight, prevents tolerance. Gloves keep the nurse from absorbing the drug. Sitting prevents a fall.

options.text: Swallow the sublingual tablet with water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sublingual tablets dissolve under the tongue and are not swallowed.

options.text: Sit down before taking a dose
options.rationale: Light, heat and air weaken the tablets, so they stay in the dark glass bottle. A daily nitrate free period, often overnight, prevents tolerance. Gloves keep the nurse from absorbing the drug. Sitting prevents a fall.

questions.takeaway: Dark bottle, nitrate free period, rotate, gloves, sit.
questions.strategy: Each correct point protects the drug, the patient or the nurse.

questions.stem: How does aspirin prevent a myocardial infarction?

options.text: It keeps platelets from clumping on plaque
options.rationale: When plaque cracks, platelets stick to it and form a clot that can block the artery. Aspirin blocks the enzyme platelets need to clump, for the life of the platelet. That is why it is given at the first sign of a possible MI.

options.text: It blocks clotting factors made by the liver
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes warfarin and similar anticoagulants.

options.text: It lowers LDL cholesterol
options.rationale: Near miss concept Statins lower LDL.

options.text: It dissolves existing clots in the coronary arteries
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thrombolytics dissolve clots.

questions.takeaway: Aspirin = antiplatelet.
questions.strategy: Separate antiplatelet, anticoagulant and thrombolytic.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about aspirin for suspected MI.
questions.sentence: For suspected MI the nurse gives aspirin per order as a [[1]] tablet so it is absorbed fast. The main adverse effect to watch for is [[2]]. Ringing in the ears suggests [[3]].

options.text: chewable, non enteric coated
enteric coated, swallowed whole
extended release
constipation
bleeding, especially in the gut
high potassium
a normal effect
an allergy
aspirin toxicity

questions.takeaway: Chewing a non enteric coated tablet gets aspirin into the blood within minutes. Enteric coating delays it. Aspirin raises the risk of bleeding, especially in the stomach. Tinnitus is a sign of toxicity. Suspected MI: chew it. Watch for bleeding.
questions.strategy: Speed matters in an MI.

questions.stem: Why must a patient with a new coronary stent not stop clopidogrel on their own?

options.text: It raises the blood pressure when stopped
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rebound pressure is a beta blocker problem.

options.text: The stent can clot, causing an MI
options.rationale: Platelets stick readily to a new stent. Clopidogrel with aspirin keeps them from clotting inside it. Stopping early can cause stent thrombosis, which is a sudden MI. Only the cardiologist decides when to stop.

options.text: It causes withdrawal seizures
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clopidogrel does not cause seizures.

options.text: It is the only drug that lowers cholesterol
options.rationale: Near miss concept Statins lower cholesterol.

questions.takeaway: Stent: do not stop clopidogrel without the cardiologist.
questions.strategy: Find the catastrophic result of stopping.

questions.stem: How does atorvastatin lower the risk of MI?

options.text: It slows the heart rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a beta blocker.

options.text: It dilates the coronary arteries during an episode of angina
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a nitrate.

options.text: It lowers LDL production in the liver and stabilizes plaque
options.rationale: Statins block HMG CoA reductase, the liver enzyme that makes cholesterol. LDL falls, and plaque becomes more stable and less likely to rupture and trigger a clot. They do nothing for chest pain today.

options.text: It keeps platelets from clumping
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is aspirin or clopidogrel.

questions.takeaway: Statin: LDL down, plaque stable, not for acute pain.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the drug treats pain now or prevents the next event.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings a patient on a statin should report.

options.text: Unexplained muscle pain
options.rationale: Statins can injure muscle. Pain, weakness and dark urine can mean rhabdomyolysis, where muscle breakdown products damage the kidneys. Statins can also injure the liver, so jaundice is reported and liver enzymes are checked.

options.text: Dark, tea colored urine
options.rationale: Statins can injure muscle. Pain, weakness and dark urine can mean rhabdomyolysis, where muscle breakdown products damage the kidneys. Statins can also injure the liver, so jaundice is reported and liver enzymes are checked.

options.text: Yellowing of the skin
options.rationale: Statins can injure muscle. Pain, weakness and dark urine can mean rhabdomyolysis, where muscle breakdown products damage the kidneys. Statins can also injure the liver, so jaundice is reported and liver enzymes are checked.

options.text: Mild headache on the first day
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A mild headache early on is not a statin warning sign.

options.text: Muscle weakness
options.rationale: Statins can injure muscle. Pain, weakness and dark urine can mean rhabdomyolysis, where muscle breakdown products damage the kidneys. Statins can also injure the liver, so jaundice is reported and liver enzymes are checked.

options.text: Dry cough
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dry cough is an ACE inhibitor effect.

questions.takeaway: Statins: muscles and liver.
questions.strategy: Group the correct options by organ.

questions.stem: A patient reports chest pain while walking. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG
Stop the activity and have the patient sit or lie down
Notify the provider
Assess the pain and take vital signs

questions.takeaway: Stopping activity lowers oxygen demand right away. Assessing the pain and vital signs tells you how sick the patient is and whether nitroglycerin is safe. A 12 lead ECG within 10 minutes shows whether this is an MI. Then the provider is notified with data. Stop, assess, ECG, notify.
questions.strategy: Lower demand first, then gather data, then report.

questions.stem: When is oxygen given to a patient with chest pain?

options.text: Only when the SpO2 is low, per order
options.rationale: Oxygen is given when the saturation is low, commonly under 90 percent, per order. Extra oxygen in a patient with a normal saturation does not improve outcomes.

options.text: Only after nitroglycerin has failed to relieve the pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oxygen depends on saturation, not on the nitrate response.

options.text: Only when the patient asks for it
options.rationale: Near miss concept The decision is based on saturation, not request.

options.text: To every patient with chest pain
options.rationale: Absolute language Routine oxygen in a patient with a normal saturation does not help and may harm.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen for low SpO2, not for every chest pain.
questions.strategy: Watch for always and every.

questions.stem: A patient has new chest pain rated 7 of 10. Blood pressure is 86/52 and heart rate is 104. Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL as needed is ordered. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it with the patient standing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Standing makes hypotension worse.

options.text: Give it, since the pain is severe
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Severe pain does not make the drug safe at this pressure.

options.text: Hold it and notify the provider
options.rationale: With a systolic under 90, nitroglycerin can drop the pressure further and reduce flow to the heart. The nurse holds it, obtains the ECG and notifies the provider.

options.text: Give half a tablet
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Splitting the dose is not a nursing decision.

questions.takeaway: Chest pain plus systolic under 90: hold the nitro.
questions.strategy: Check the pressure before the nitro, every time.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain has a blood pressure of 132/80. While preparing nitroglycerin, the nurse learns the patient took tadalafil yesterday evening. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give half the usual dose
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Dose changes are not the nurse's decision.

options.text: Give the nitroglycerin, since the pressure is normal
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A normal pressure now does not prevent the severe drop the combination causes.

options.text: Hold it and tell the provider about the tadalafil
options.rationale: Tadalafil lasts up to 48 hours and with a nitrate can cause severe hypotension. The nurse holds the nitrate, tells the provider and continues the chest pain workup.

options.text: Give it and recheck the pressure in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature Checking after the drop is too late.

questions.takeaway: Ask about these drugs before every nitrate.
questions.strategy: The interaction, not the current number, decides.

questions.stem: A patient on atorvastatin 80 mg reports aching thighs for 4 days without exercise and urine the color of tea. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient this is expected and to take the dose at night
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem This is not expected; it may be muscle breakdown.

options.text: Hold the statin and notify the provider
options.rationale: Unexplained muscle pain with dark urine suggests rhabdomyolysis. The nurse holds the statin and notifies the provider, who will check a creatine kinase and kidney function.

options.text: Suggest more exercise to stretch the muscles
options.rationale: Near miss concept Exercise adds muscle injury.

options.text: Advise ibuprofen for the aches
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Pain relief hides the problem and NSAIDs can stress the kidneys.

questions.takeaway: Statin plus muscle pain plus dark urine: hold and report.
questions.strategy: Dark urine moves this from side effect to emergency.

questions.stem: A patient who had a coronary stent placed 2 months ago says, "My dentist wants me off my clopidogrel before a tooth extraction next week." Which response is best?

options.text: "Stop it 5 days before the extraction as the dentist says."
options.rationale: Institution as rationale The dentist's request does not account for the stent risk.

options.text: "Your cardiologist must decide; stopping can clot the stent."
options.rationale: A new stent depends on dual antiplatelet therapy. The cardiologist and dentist decide together whether and when it can be held. The nurse explains why and connects them.

options.text: "Keep taking it and do not mention it to the dentist."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hiding it from the dentist is unsafe; they need to plan for bleeding.

options.text: "Switch to aspirin alone the week of the procedure."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the regimen is not a nursing decision.

questions.takeaway: Stent plus procedure: the cardiologist decides.
questions.strategy: Pick the response that routes the decision to the right provider.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews sublingual nitroglycerin teaching. Which statement shows the patient understands?

options.text: "I will keep the tablets in my weekly pill organizer so I always have them handy."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Light and air weaken the tablets; they belong in the dark glass bottle.

options.text: "I will stand up and walk it off after the tablet."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sitting prevents a fall; activity raises demand.

options.text: "I will take all 3 tablets before calling 911."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Waiting for 3 tablets delays care for a possible MI by 15 minutes.

options.text: "If the pain is not better 5 minutes after the first, I will call 911."
options.rationale: If the pain is not better 5 minutes after the first tablet, the patient calls 911, then may continue up to 3 tablets. Tablets stay in the dark glass bottle, and the patient sits down.

questions.takeaway: First tablet, 5 minutes, not better, call 911.
questions.strategy: Evaluate teaching by finding the safe behavior.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected MI has an order for aspirin 324 mg PO now. The dispensing cabinet has enteric coated aspirin 325 mg and chewable aspirin 81 mg tablets. What should the nurse give?

options.text: Four chewable 81 mg tablets, chewed
options.rationale: Four chewable 81 mg tablets give 324 mg that is absorbed within minutes. Enteric coating delays absorption, and crushing it defeats the coating.

options.text: Two chewable 81 mg tablets, since less is safer
options.rationale: Near miss concept 162 mg is less than the 324 mg ordered.

options.text: One enteric coated tablet, crushed in water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Enteric coated tablets are not crushed.

options.text: One enteric coated 325 mg tablet, swallowed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Enteric coating delays absorption when speed matters.

questions.takeaway: Suspected MI: chewable, not enteric coated.
questions.strategy: Check both the dose and the form.

questions.stem: A patient with known CAD develops crushing chest pain rated 8 of 10 with sweating and nausea while at rest. Blood pressure is 142/88, heart rate is 98 and SpO2 is 96% on room air. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 6 L by nasal cannula
Have the patient walk to the bathroom
Give aspirin to chew per order
Hold all medications until the troponin results
Obtain a 12 lead ECG within 10 minutes
Stable angina
Pericarditis
Gastroesophageal reflux
Acute coronary syndrome
Blood pressure before each nitroglycerin dose
Pain rating after each intervention
Serum potassium
Daily weight
Peak flow

questions.takeaway: Crushing pain at rest with sweating and nausea is acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. The nurse obtains an ECG within 10 minutes and gives chewable aspirin per order. With a normal saturation, oxygen is not needed. Pain and blood pressure guide each nitroglycerin dose. Pain at rest is not stable angina.
questions.strategy: Rest pain plus sweating changes the condition.

questions.stem: What causes the symptoms of heart failure?

options.text: The coronary arteries close, so heart muscle dies
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes an MI, which can cause heart failure.

options.text: The kidneys stop making any urine at all, so fluid builds up throughout the body
options.rationale: Near miss concept The kidneys hold fluid in heart failure because of low flow, but they have not stopped.

options.text: The heart beats too fast to fill, so blood pools in the arms
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fast rate can worsen failure, but pooling in the arms is not the mechanism.

options.text: The heart cannot pump enough, so fluid backs up into the lungs and tissues
options.rationale: A weak or stiff heart moves less blood forward. Blood backs up behind the failing side: into the lungs (crackles, dyspnea) or into the body (edema, weight gain). Low flow to the kidneys activates RAAS, which holds even more fluid.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure = backup plus RAAS holding fluid.
questions.strategy: Sort every heart failure drug into feel better now or live longer.

questions.stem: Match each drug to its main role in heart failure.
questions.takeaway: Loop diuretics remove fluid and make the patient feel better quickly. The protective drugs block the hormones that strain the heart: ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI, a beta blocker, spironolactone and an SGLT2 inhibitor. They lower workload, slow damage and reduce deaths. Loops for now; the other four groups for later.
questions.strategy: Sort every heart failure drug into feel better now or live longer.

questions.stem: Select all of the drug groups used to protect the heart long term in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

options.text: Loop diuretic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Loops relieve symptoms but do not lengthen life.

options.text: Beta blocker such as carvedilol
options.rationale: Four groups protect the heart: ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI; a heart failure beta blocker; an aldosterone blocker; and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Loops relieve congestion on top of them.

options.text: ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI
options.rationale: Four groups protect the heart: ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI; a heart failure beta blocker; an aldosterone blocker; and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Loops relieve congestion on top of them.

options.text: Diltiazem
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diltiazem weakens contraction and is avoided in reduced ejection fraction.

options.text: SGLT2 inhibitor
options.rationale: Four groups protect the heart: ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI; a heart failure beta blocker; an aldosterone blocker; and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Loops relieve congestion on top of them.

options.text: Aldosterone blocker such as spironolactone
options.rationale: Four groups protect the heart: ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI; a heart failure beta blocker; an aldosterone blocker; and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Loops relieve congestion on top of them.

questions.takeaway: Four protectors plus a loop for symptoms.
questions.strategy: Sort every heart failure drug into feel better now or live longer.

questions.stem: What is sacubitril/valsartan?

options.text: An ACE inhibitor combined with a loop diuretic in a single tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept It contains no ACE inhibitor or diuretic.

options.text: An ARB combined with a drug that keeps natriuretic peptides active
options.rationale: Sacubitril/valsartan is an ARNI: an angiotensin receptor blocker (valsartan) plus a neprilysin inhibitor (sacubitril). Neprilysin breaks down natriuretic peptides, the hormones that help the body get rid of sodium and water and relax vessels. Blocking it keeps them working longer.

options.text: A beta blocker that also relaxes vessels
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes carvedilol.

options.text: A calcium channel blocker for the failing heart
options.rationale: Near miss concept Calcium channel blockers are not part of this drug.

questions.takeaway: ARNI = ARB plus neprilysin inhibitor.
questions.strategy: Split the combination into its two parts.

questions.stem: Why is sacubitril/valsartan never given with lisinopril?

options.text: The combination raises the risk of angioedema
options.rationale: Neprilysin and ACE both help break down bradykinin. Blocking both lets bradykinin build up and raises the risk of angioedema. Lisinopril is stopped at least 36 hours before the first ARNI dose.

options.text: Lisinopril blocks the absorption of sacubitril
options.rationale: Near miss concept The problem is not absorption.

options.text: The combination causes severe hypokalemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Both raise, not lower, potassium.

options.text: It does not matter as long as doses are spaced
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spacing does not make it safe; a 36 hour washout is needed.

questions.takeaway: ARNI and ACE inhibitor: never together, 36 hours apart.
questions.strategy: Two blocks on bradykinin breakdown means angioedema.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings the nurse monitors for in a patient on sacubitril/valsartan.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not affect glucose.

options.text: Hypotension
options.rationale: As an ARB plus a drug that relaxes vessels, it can cause low pressure, high potassium, kidney changes and angioedema.

options.text: Hyperkalemia
options.rationale: As an ARB plus a drug that relaxes vessels, it can cause low pressure, high potassium, kidney changes and angioedema.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not slow the heart.

options.text: Swelling of the lips or tongue
options.rationale: As an ARB plus a drug that relaxes vessels, it can cause low pressure, high potassium, kidney changes and angioedema.

options.text: Rising creatinine
options.rationale: As an ARB plus a drug that relaxes vessels, it can cause low pressure, high potassium, kidney changes and angioedema.

questions.takeaway: ARNI: pressure, potassium, kidneys, angioedema.
questions.strategy: Combine what you know about ARBs with the bradykinin risk.

questions.stem: Which beta blocker order should the nurse clarify for a patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?

options.text: Metoprolol succinate 12.5 mg PO daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Metoprolol succinate is the proven form for heart failure.

options.text: Carvedilol 3.125 mg PO BID
options.rationale: Near miss concept Carvedilol is a proven heart failure beta blocker.

options.text: Bisoprolol 1.25 mg PO daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bisoprolol is a proven heart failure beta blocker.

options.text: Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO BID
options.rationale: Only carvedilol, bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate have been shown to lower deaths in heart failure. Metoprolol tartrate is the short acting form and is not the evidence based choice, so the nurse clarifies.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure beta blockers: carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate.
questions.strategy: Separate the two metoprolol salts.

questions.stem: How are beta blockers started in heart failure?

options.text: At a full dose from the first day to protect the heart quickly
options.rationale: Near miss concept A full dose can worsen failure by reducing the force of the heart.

options.text: At a low dose, raised slowly, once the patient is stable
options.rationale: Beta blockers reduce the force of contraction at first, so the patient may feel more tired. Over weeks to months they let the heart recover. They start low, go up slowly and are started when the patient is stable, not during an acute flare.

options.text: Only during an acute episode of fluid overload
options.rationale: Near miss concept They are not started during acute decompensation.

options.text: As needed when the heart rate is high
options.rationale: Near miss concept They are scheduled daily drugs.

questions.takeaway: Start low, go slow, once stable.
questions.strategy: Ask what a full dose would do on day one.

questions.stem: How does empagliflozin help a patient with heart failure?

options.text: It raises insulin release from the pancreas
options.rationale: Near miss concept SGLT2 inhibitors do not work through insulin.

options.text: It makes the kidneys pass glucose and sodium in the urine
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors block glucose and sodium reabsorption in the kidney, so more leaves in the urine with water. This mild fluid loss and other effects lower heart failure admissions and deaths, even in patients without diabetes.

options.text: It blocks the angiotensin II receptor in the walls of the vessels
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is an ARB.

options.text: It slows the heart rate and lowers oxygen demand
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a beta blocker.

questions.takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitor: glucose and sodium out in the urine; helps the heart with or without diabetes.
questions.strategy: Name what leaves in the urine.

questions.stem: Select all of the adverse effects the nurse teaches about for dapagliflozin.

options.text: Genital yeast infections
options.rationale: Glucose in the urine feeds yeast and bacteria, so genital infections and urinary infections rise. Fluid loss can cause dehydration and low pressure. Rarely, ketoacidosis occurs even with a normal glucose. Teach hygiene, fluids and to report nausea, vomiting or belly pain.

options.text: Urinary tract infections
options.rationale: Glucose in the urine feeds yeast and bacteria, so genital infections and urinary infections rise. Fluid loss can cause dehydration and low pressure. Rarely, ketoacidosis occurs even with a normal glucose. Teach hygiene, fluids and to report nausea, vomiting or belly pain.

options.text: Dehydration and low blood pressure
options.rationale: Glucose in the urine feeds yeast and bacteria, so genital infections and urinary infections rise. Fluid loss can cause dehydration and low pressure. Rarely, ketoacidosis occurs even with a normal glucose. Teach hygiene, fluids and to report nausea, vomiting or belly pain.

options.text: Weight gain from fluid retention
options.rationale: Near miss concept These drugs cause fluid loss, not retention.

options.text: Ketoacidosis, which is rare
options.rationale: Glucose in the urine feeds yeast and bacteria, so genital infections and urinary infections rise. Fluid loss can cause dehydration and low pressure. Rarely, ketoacidosis occurs even with a normal glucose. Teach hygiene, fluids and to report nausea, vomiting or belly pain.

options.text: Dry cough
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cough is an ACE inhibitor effect.

questions.takeaway: SGLT2: infections, fluid loss, rare ketoacidosis.
questions.strategy: Trace the effects from sugar in the urine.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about heart failure drug monitoring.
questions.sentence: A patient on furosemide, spironolactone and lisinopril needs close monitoring of [[1]], because the loop lowers it while the other two [[2]] it. The best daily measure of fluid status is [[3]].

options.text: sodium
glucose
potassium
raise
lower
do not change
intake alone
daily weight
edema grade

questions.takeaway: Loops push potassium down. Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors push it up. The net effect is unpredictable, so potassium is checked often. Daily weight on the same scale at the same time is the most reliable fluid measure. Mixed potassium effects: check the potassium.
questions.strategy: Add the potassium arrows of each drug.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure took lisinopril at 0800 today. The provider stopped lisinopril and ordered sacubitril/valsartan, first dose tonight at 2000. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give half the dose tonight and the full dose tomorrow
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is not the nurse's decision.

options.text: Give the first dose at 2000 as ordered
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Following the time on the order ignores a dangerous interaction.

options.text: Clarify the start time, since 36 hours must pass
options.rationale: Only 12 hours will have passed since the last lisinopril. Giving the ARNI this soon raises the risk of angioedema. The nurse clarifies so the first dose is at least 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose.

options.text: Give it, then watch the lips and tongue all night
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Watching for angioedema does not prevent it.

questions.takeaway: ACE inhibitor to ARNI: 36 hours apart.
questions.strategy: Calculate the gap between the two drugs.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure started carvedilol 3.125 mg BID 10 days ago. The patient says, "I feel more tired since I started it. Should I stop it?" Weight and lungs are unchanged and the heart rate is 66. Which response is best?

options.text: "Take it every other day to cut the tiredness."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the schedule is the provider's decision.

options.text: "Feeling this tired means your heart failure is getting worse again."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stable weight and lungs argue against worsening failure.

options.text: "Yes, stop it until you feel better."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stopping a beta blocker suddenly can cause rebound.

options.text: "Tiredness is common early; keep taking it and tell your provider."
options.rationale: Fatigue is common in the first weeks while the heart adjusts. With stable weight, lungs and heart rate, the nurse encourages the patient to keep taking it and reports the fatigue.

questions.takeaway: Early fatigue on a heart failure beta blocker: keep taking it and report.
questions.strategy: Check stable data before calling it worsening.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure started empagliflozin 3 weeks ago and reports genital itching and a white discharge. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to stop the drug
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Stopping it is the provider's decision; the infection is usually treated and the drug continued.

options.text: Report it as a likely yeast infection from the drug
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors put glucose in the urine, which feeds yeast. The nurse reports it, teaches hygiene and encourages fluids. The infection is treated and the drug is often continued.

options.text: Tell the patient it is unrelated to the medicine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glucose in the urine makes yeast infections common.

options.text: Advise drinking less water so the patient urinates less often
options.rationale: Near miss concept Less water worsens dehydration and infection risk.

questions.takeaway: SGLT2 plus genital itching: report, teach hygiene.
questions.strategy: Link the symptom to the mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with acute decompensated heart failure has crackles to the mid lungs, SpO2 89% on 4 L and a blood pressure of 92/60. A new order reads carvedilol 6.25 mg PO BID, start now. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it and recheck the pressure in 1 hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Checking after the dose is too late if the failure worsens.

options.text: Give it, since carvedilol protects the heart
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data True long term, but not during acute decompensation.

options.text: Clarify the order before giving the first dose
options.rationale: Starting a beta blocker during acute decompensation can weaken the heart further and drop a low pressure. Beta blockers are started once the patient is stable. The nurse clarifies.

options.text: Give it with the IV furosemide
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Treating congestion does not make starting a beta blocker now safe.

questions.takeaway: Acute flare plus low pressure: do not start the beta blocker.
questions.strategy: Timing matters as much as the drug.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure reports needing three pillows to sleep, has gained 4 lb in 2 days, and has crackles in both bases and 2+ ankle edema. SpO2 is 91% on room air and blood pressure is 148/90. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Encourage 2 liters of oral fluid today
Give IV furosemide per order
Give the morning carvedilol at a double dose
Keep the patient flat to rest the heart
Place the patient in high Fowler position
Acute heart failure exacerbation with fluid overload
Dehydration
Pneumonia
Hypokalemia
Blood glucose
Serum calcium
Lung sounds and SpO2
Daily weight
Pupil response

questions.takeaway: Orthopnea, rapid weight gain, crackles and edema mean fluid overload. The nurse sits the patient up, gives IV furosemide per order and monitors weight, lung sounds and saturation. Potassium is also checked after diuresis. Fluid overload: upright, loop, weight, lungs.
questions.strategy: Match monitors to the problem the actions treat.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure takes the drugs below. Match each drug to the finding that should make the nurse hold it and call.
questions.takeaway: Spironolactone raises potassium, so a level of 5.8 is the hold. Carvedilol and bisoprolol slow the heart. Furosemide can remove too much fluid and drop the pressure. Each hold finding matches what the drug does too much of. Hold for what the drug pushes too far.
questions.strategy: Match each drug's main danger.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has these 0900 findings: apical pulse 56, blood pressure 118/70, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, weight down 1 lb. The order set includes lisinopril 10 mg daily and valsartan 80 mg daily. Carvedilol has a hold parameter of heart rate under 60. Decide what to do with each drug.
questions.takeaway: Carvedilol is held because the pulse is under its parameter. Furosemide is held because the potassium of 3.2 will fall further. Valsartan with lisinopril blocks the same chain twice, so the order is clarified. Atorvastatin and empagliflozin have no findings against them today. Each drug gets its own check.
questions.strategy: For each drug, ask: what does it push, where is that value now, and is the order itself safe?

questions.stem: At the start of the 0900 medication pass, the nurse has four patients. Place them in the order the nurse should see them.

options.text: A patient on spironolactone whose potassium is 5.1 mEq/L
A patient on furosemide asking for help to the bathroom, who is steady on their feet
A patient on lisinopril with new swelling of the lips and a hoarse voice
A patient due for nitroglycerin patch removal at 0900

questions.takeaway: Angioedema with a hoarse voice threatens the airway and comes first. A patient on a diuretic who needs the bathroom is a fall risk if left waiting. The patch removal is time based but not dangerous if a few minutes late. A potassium of 5.1 is just above range and is reviewed with the provider at the routine check. Airway, then safety, then time, then numbers.
questions.strategy: Rank by what harms the patient first.

questions.stem: A patient with moderate persistent asthma develops atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 132. Which rate control drug should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Propranolol
options.rationale: Near miss concept Propranolol is nonselective and can trigger bronchospasm in asthma.

options.text: Diltiazem
options.rationale: Rate control uses a beta blocker or diltiazem. With asthma, nonselective beta blockers are avoided, so diltiazem slows AV conduction without affecting the airways.

options.text: Carvedilol
options.rationale: Near miss concept Carvedilol is also nonselective.

options.text: Nitroglycerin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nitroglycerin does not control the rate.

questions.takeaway: Asthma plus atrial fibrillation: diltiazem.
questions.strategy: Rule out by the second condition.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure takes sacubitril/valsartan, spironolactone and furosemide. Potassium is 5.6 mEq/L, blood pressure is 112/68 and heart rate is 74. All three are due. Which drug should the nurse hold first?

options.text: Spironolactone, since it raises potassium
options.rationale: Spironolactone and the ARB in the ARNI both raise potassium, and spironolactone is the drug most often held for hyperkalemia. Furosemide lowers potassium. The nurse holds spironolactone, notifies the provider and asks about the ARNI.

options.text: None, since the blood pressure is normal
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A normal pressure does not cancel a high potassium.

options.text: Sacubitril/valsartan, since it lowers pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept The pressure is fine; the potassium is the problem.

options.text: Furosemide, since it changes potassium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Furosemide lowers potassium, so it does not add to the problem.

questions.takeaway: High potassium: hold the potassium sparing drug first.
questions.strategy: Find the drug pushing the lab the wrong way.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has had a dry cough for 2 months on lisinopril. Lungs are clear. Complete the statement.
questions.sentence: The cough is most likely caused by [[1]]. The nurse anticipates a switch to [[2]], and after the switch the nurse continues to monitor [[3]].

options.text: bradykinin buildup from the ACE inhibitor
a viral infection
fluid in the lungs
furosemide
metoprolol
losartan
peak flow and SpO2
potassium and creatinine
blood glucose only

questions.takeaway: ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown, causing a dry cough. An ARB keeps the kidney protection without the cough. ARBs still raise potassium and can change creatinine, so both are monitored. ACE cough in kidney disease: switch to an ARB, keep watching potassium and creatinine.
questions.strategy: For each drug, ask: what does it push, where is that value now, and is the order itself safe?

questions.stem: A patient is being discharged after a coronary stent on aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol succinate, atorvastatin and nitroglycerin SL. Select all of the statements that show the patient needs more teaching.

options.text: "I will stop the clopidogrel once my chest pain is gone."
options.rationale: Stopping clopidogrel early can clot the stent. Changing a metoprolol dose is the provider's decision, and the succinate form is extended release, so it is not crushed. The other statements show correct understanding.

options.text: "I will cut my metoprolol in half if my pulse feels slow."
options.rationale: Stopping clopidogrel early can clot the stent. Changing a metoprolol dose is the provider's decision, and the succinate form is extended release, so it is not crushed. The other statements show correct understanding.

options.text: "I will report any new muscle pain or dark urine to my provider right away."
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is correct statin teaching.

options.text: "I will sit down before I take a nitroglycerin."
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is correct nitroglycerin teaching.

options.text: "I will crush my metoprolol if it is hard to swallow."
options.rationale: Stopping clopidogrel early can clot the stent. Changing a metoprolol dose is the provider's decision, and the succinate form is extended release, so it is not crushed. The other statements show correct understanding.

options.text: "I will tell my dentist I take two blood thinners."
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is correct antiplatelet teaching.

questions.takeaway: Stent, extended release and dose changes are where teaching fails.
questions.strategy: In a needs more teaching item, the correct answers are the wrong statements.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes a patient's metoprolol succinate ER 100 mg was crushed and given through a feeding tube 30 minutes ago. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Call pharmacy to ask about the form
options.rationale: Correct but premature Pharmacy input is useful later; the patient may already be bradycardic.

options.text: Document that the tablet was crushed
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documentation follows assessment.

options.text: File an incident report
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The report comes after the patient is safe.

options.text: Check the apical pulse and blood pressure
options.rationale: Crushing an extended release beta blocker releases the whole dose at once, so bradycardia and hypotension can develop quickly. The nurse assesses first, then notifies the provider, documents and reports.

questions.takeaway: Error with a cardiac drug: assess what it lowers.
questions.strategy: Patient first.

questions.stem: A 78 year old with hypertension started hydrochlorothiazide 6 weeks ago and lisinopril 2 weeks ago. Today the patient reports a hot, swollen, painful big toe. Uric acid is 9.4 mg/dL, potassium is 3.9 mEq/L and blood pressure is 128/76. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids unless restricted
Apply heat and have the patient walk on it
Hold the lisinopril for the joint pain
Report the joint pain and uric acid to the provider
Increase dietary potassium
Cellulitis from a foot wound
Gout flare linked to the thiazide
Hyperkalemia from the ACE inhibitor
Hypokalemia from the thiazide
Serum calcium only
Heart rate before each dose
Pain and swelling of the joint
Peak flow
Uric acid level

questions.takeaway: Thiazides raise uric acid and can trigger gout. A hot, swollen big toe with a high uric acid is a gout flare. Potassium is normal. The nurse reports it, encourages fluids if allowed and monitors the uric acid and the joint. Lisinopril is not the cause. Thiazide plus hot big toe: gout.
questions.strategy: Link the new symptom to the drug known for it.
